title: Spanish at Home
audience: A parent and their teenage daughter (plus a brother and Monty the dog)
pronunciation_guide: English-friendly respelling for Spain (Castilian) Spanish, generated from the Spanish by tools/phonetic.mjs. Vowels: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. th = c/z, h = j and soft g (a strong, breathy h), b = b/v, y = ll, ny = ñ, rr = rolled r. CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable.

phrases.note: Levántate comes from levantarse, 'to get up' (literally 'to lift yourself'). The -te stuck on the end means 'yourself'.
Handy pattern: Es hora de + verb = 'It's time to...'. Try es hora de cenar (time for dinner) or es hora de irse (time to go). The h in hora is silent.
Sal comes from salir (to go out/leave). It's the short 'you do it' command form, and sal de means 'get out of'.
Adding ya to the end of an order means 'right now!' and makes it sound more impatient than ahora.
Venga is what people in Spain say all the time for 'come on'. Put it in front of any order to hurry someone along without sounding harsh.
Llegar tarde means 'to arrive late', which is how Spanish says 'to be late'. Vas a + verb = 'you're going to...'.
Here ya means 'already'. Word for word it's 'already you arrive late'. Don't forget the ll sounds like the y in 'yes'.
Despierta is for a girl. Say despierto to a boy. It uses estás because being awake is a state that changes.
Word for word it's 'Have you slept well?'. In Spain people use has + verb for things that happened this morning or earlier today.

phrases.en: What time did you go to sleep?
phrases.note: Dormirse (with te) means 'to fall asleep', while plain dormir just means 'to sleep'. ¿A qué hora...? = 'At what time...?'
Spanish has a verb for 'to shower yourself': ducharse. So you don't 'have' a shower, you 'showered yourself': te has duchado.
Ve a + verb = 'Go and...'. Ve is the tiny command form of ir (to go). Reuse it: ve a vestirte, ve a por tus zapatos.
Vístete comes from vestirse, 'to dress yourself'. The -te on the end is 'yourself'. Said on its own it can sound quite firm.
Vestida is for a girl. Say vestido to a boy. Handy before opening a bedroom door!
Spanish 'washes' teeth (lavarse los dientes) rather than brushing them. It also says los dientes ('the teeth'), not 'your teeth', because te already shows whose.
Arreglar means 'to fix' or 'sort out', so arreglarse el pelo is 'to sort out your hair'. Arreglarse on its own means 'to get ready'.
Spanish sneaks in an extra lo ('it') before tienes when todo is the thing you have. Word for word: 'It you have all?'
For where something is, always use estar (están), never ser. In Spain the z in zapatos is said like 'th'.
Watch the accent: está (is) versus esta (this). Tu with no accent means 'your', and tú with one means 'you'.

phrases.es: No te olvides de la mochila.
phrases.ph: noh teh ohl-BEE-dehs deh lah moh-CHEE-lah
phrases.note: Reusable pattern: No te olvides de + thing = 'Don't forget (the)...'. A mochila is a rucksack, the usual school bag.

phrases.es: No te olvides de la comida.
phrases.ph: noh teh ohl-BEE-dehs deh lah koh-MEE-dah
phrases.note: In Spain la comida means both 'food' and 'lunch', the big midday meal. Spanish says la ('the') where English says 'your'.
In Spain a mobile phone is el móvil. In Latin America it's el celular. As usual, 'your' just becomes el ('the').
Llaves = keys; one key is una llave. Two tricky sounds: ll is said like the y in 'yes', and the v is soft, almost like a b.

phrases.en: What time do you need to leave?
phrases.ph: ah keh OH-rah TYEH-nehs keh sah-LEER
phrases.note: Tienes que + verb = 'you have to...'. It's one of the most useful patterns there is: tienes que salir, tienes que comer, tienes que estudiar.

phrases.en: What time do you need to be there?
phrases.es: ¿A qué hora tienes que estar allí?
phrases.ph: ah keh OH-rah TYEH-nehs keh ehs-TAHR ah-YEE
phrases.note: Allí means 'there' (somewhere away from both of you). Estar is the 'to be' for places, so estar allí = 'to be there'.
Lista is for a girl. Say listo to a boy. Careful: with ser instead (eres lista) it means 'you're clever'!
Casi = 'nearly', and ya casi is like 'just about'. Lista is for a girl, so ask a boy ¿Ya casi estás listo?
Venga is very Spain. It can mean 'come on!', 'hurry up!' or even 'OK then'. Say ¡Venga, venga! to really hurry someone.
Literally 'give yourself hurry': prisa means 'hurry' or 'rush'. Tengo prisa = 'I'm in a hurry'.
Irse (here irnos, 'us to go') means 'to leave' or 'go off', while plain ir is just 'to go'. Tenemos que = 'we have to'.
No word for 'for' is needed: esperar already means 'to wait for'. Te ('you') goes before the verb.
Todos ('all of them') is how Spanish says 'everyone' here, so the verb is plural: están, not está.
Nos vamos = 'we're off'. Spanish often uses the present for plans that will happen soon. Cinco starts with a 'th' sound in Spain.
Nos vamos ya is the 'final warning' version. Ya on the end means 'right now', and it's firmer than ahora.
Spanish 'goes up' into a car: subir (to go up) + al (a + el) coche. Getting out is bajar: baja del coche.
It's always plural in Spain: buenos días, literally 'good days'. People use it until lunchtime, then switch to buenas tardes.
Despertador (alarm clock) comes from despertar, 'to wake up'. Sonar = 'to ring' or 'make a sound'.
Oído = 'heard', from oír. The accent on the í means you say the o and the í separately. Oír is hearing, and escuchar is listening.
Volver a + verb = 'to do again', so no te vuelvas a dormir is 'don't fall asleep again'. It's perfect for a snoozer.
El baño is the bathroom (and the toilet). Libre = 'free' as in not in use, and ocupado means 'someone's in there'.
One verb does the whole job: desayunar = 'to have breakfast'. Ya he desayunado = 'I've already had breakfast'.

phrases.en: Have some breakfast before you go.
phrases.note: Antes de + verb = 'before ...ing'. The verb stays in its basic form, so irte ('you going') keeps te on the end.
Ponerse = 'to put on' clothes. Ponte is 'put on (yourself)', and you just swap the item: ponte el abrigo, ponte la sudadera.
Abrigo is a warm coat. For a light jacket say la chaqueta. The opposite is quítate el abrigo ('take your coat off').
Literally 'Do you have the uniform clean?' Limpio matches uniforme. For a feminine thing it's limpia: ¿Tienes la camisa limpia?
Cinco minutos más = 'five more minutes'. In Spanish más usually comes after the thing: un poco más, un día más.
Vete = 'go away', from irse (to leave). Quite blunt — fine with family, rude with anyone else.
¡Fuera! literally means 'outside!' and works as a sharp 'get out!'. Short, loud and a bit rude.
Sal = 'get out', from salir. Cuarto is the everyday Spain word for bedroom — habitación is a bit more formal.
Cansada is for a girl — a boy says cansado. Use estar for how you feel right now.
Muerta means 'dead'; add -ísima to make it extreme: 'I'm totally dead'. A boy says muertísimo.
Ya here means 'already', so this is 'I'm already up!'. Levantada is for a girl — a boy says levantado.
Starting with que makes it sound fed up, like 'I SAID I'm getting up!'. Handy for any repeated nag.
Deja de + verb = 'stop doing something'. Swap the verb: deja de cantar, deja de molestar.
No encuentro = 'I can't find'. Spanish doesn't need 'can' here — just 'I don't find'.
Cepillo = brush. For a hairbrush, cepillo on its own is enough; a toothbrush is a cepillo de dientes.
Déjame en paz = literally 'leave me in peace'. The go-to way to say 'leave me alone' — a bit sharp.
Pronto means 'early' here (as well as 'soon'). In Spain people say pronto more than temprano for this.
Spanish says 'I don't have hunger': tener hambre. Same pattern for thirsty: tener sed.
¡Ya voy! = 'I'm coming!'. Spanish uses 'I go' (voy) where English says 'I'm coming'.
Apagar = to turn off; encender = to turn on. Works for lights, the telly, your phone.
Cierra = 'close', from cerrar. Its opposite is abre: abre las cortinas.
No... nada = 'not at all' / 'nothing'. Spanish happily uses two negatives together.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.note: Instituto (or insti, for short) is secondary school in Spain. Al = a + el, 'to the'.
Me encuentro mal = 'I feel unwell'. Parents may suspect this one first thing in the morning!
Hay alguien = 'there's someone'. Baño is the bathroom or the loo in Spain.

phrases.en: He's been in there for ages!
phrases.note: Lleva siglos = 'he's been ages' — siglos literally means 'centuries'. Nice bit of exaggeration about your brother.

phrases.en: Who used all the hot water?
phrases.es: ¿Quién ha gastado toda el agua caliente?
phrases.ph: kyehn ah gahs-TAH-doh TOH-dah ehl AH-gwah kah-LYEHN-teh
phrases.note: Gastar = to use up (or spend money). Agua takes el but is still feminine, so it's toda el agua caliente.

phrases.en: Can you take me in the car?
phrases.note: ¿Me llevas? = 'will you take me?'. Spain says coche for car. Add al instituto for 'to school'.
Los lunes = 'Mondays'. Days of the week have no capital letters in Spanish and don't change in the plural.
Date prisa = 'hurry up'. Spain also says ¡Venga! or ¡Espabila! to chivvy someone along.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: ¿Cuánto te queda? = literally 'how much is left for you?'. Short and very Spanish.

phrases.es: Los demás también necesitan el baño.
phrases.ph: lohs deh-MAHS tahm-BYEHN neh-theh-SEE-tahn ehl BAH-nyoh
phrases.note: Los demás = 'the others' / 'everyone else'. Very handy: piensa en los demás.
No vas a ir así = 'you're not going like that'. Así means 'like that' — very common in Spanish.
Guapa is for a girl — a boy is guapo. Spanish uses estar for how someone looks today.
Eso = 'that' (something near you); esto = 'this' (something near me).
Secador = hairdryer, from secar (to dry). Apaga = turn off.
Baja = 'turn down' (literally 'lower'). Turn it up is sube.

phrases.en: You've been in there for ages.
phrases.note: Llevas siglos = 'you've been ages'. Siglos means 'centuries' — Spaniards love this exaggeration.
Abre = 'open', from abrir. The opposite is cierra (close).

phrases.en: Put a jumper on, it's cold.
phrases.es: Ponte un jersey, que hace frío.
phrases.ph: POHN-teh oon hehr-SAY, keh AH-theh FREE-oh
phrases.note: Jersey is the Spain word for a jumper. Que here means 'because' — very common in chatty Spanish.
Falda = skirt. Demasiado = 'too' (too much); corta is feminine to match falda.
Maquillaje = makeup; maquillarse = to put makeup on. Say it gently — it can sound harsh.

phrases.en: Don't leave your towel on the floor.
phrases.es: No dejes la toalla en el suelo.
phrases.ph: noh DEH-hehs lah toh-AH-yah ehn ehl SWEH-loh
phrases.note: Suelo = floor. Dejar = to leave something somewhere. Toalla = towel.
Mum talking. Camiseta = T-shirt or top. Dad would ask ¿Esa es mi sudadera? (hoodie) instead.

phrases.en: Your clothes are on the chair.
phrases.es: Tu ropa está en la silla.
phrases.ph: too RROH-pah ehs-TAH ehn lah SEE-yah
phrases.note: Ropa = clothes, but it's singular in Spanish: la ropa está, not están.

phrases.en: It's still in the washing machine.
phrases.note: Lavadora = washing machine, from lavar (to wash). Todavía = still. Handy when she wants her favourite jeans.
Ponte = 'put on', from ponerse. Otra cosa = something else — never say una otra.
No... más = 'not any more'. Esperar means both 'to wait' and 'to hope'.
Vas bien así = 'you're fine as you are'. Perfecta is for a girl — a boy is perfecto.
Vestirse means 'to dress yourself' — the me shows you're doing it to yourself. The e changes to i in vistiendo, a common spelling twist.
Ducharse is 'to shower yourself', from la ducha (the shower). Estoy + -ando = 'I'm doing it right now'.
Estoy is used for where you are, so estoy en la ducha is 'I'm in the shower'. Swap the place: estoy en el baño, estoy en mi habitación.
Arreglar means 'to fix' or 'sort out'. Spanish says el pelo ('the hair'), not 'my hair' — the me already shows it's yours.
Maquillarse is one word for 'to put on makeup' — the makeup itself is el maquillaje. The ll sounds like an English y.
Spanish 'washes' teeth: lavarse los dientes. Again it's los dientes ('the teeth'), because the me already makes them yours.
Lista is for a girl — a boy says listo. Ready always uses estar (estoy), because it's how you are right now.

phrases.en: I'll be ready in five minutes.
phrases.note: Estaré means 'I will be'. En cinco minutos is 'in five minutes'. A boy would say estaré listo.
Short and handy. You'll also hear un momento or, very Spanish, un segundito — the -ito ending makes things sound small.
Dame is da (give) + me stuck together. Commands in Spanish often glue the 'me' onto the end, like dime (tell me).
Espera is 'wait' said to one person. To your mum and brother together it's esperad — the Spain form for 'you lot'.
Literally 'I'm already going!' Spanish uses voy (I go), not vengo (I come), when you're heading towards someone who called you.

phrases.en: I'll be there in a minute.
phrases.note: Voy is 'I'm going', which Spanish uses for 'I'm on my way'. Ahora voy ('coming now') is another common answer.
Bajar means 'to go down', so bajo is 'I'm coming down'. The opposite is subir: ya subo, 'I'm coming up'.
La ropa means 'clothes' but it's singular, so it's mi ropa and está — not mis or están.
Sudadera comes from sudar, 'to sweat' — it's a sweatshirt or hoodie. If you need to be exact, a hoodie is una sudadera con capucha.
In Spain jeans are los vaqueros — 'cowboys'! Like in English, it's always plural, so it's mis vaqueros.
Están (plural) goes with more than one thing. Trainers are las zapatillas — useful, as that's what most teenagers actually wear.
Limpio means 'clean', and its opposite is sucio (dirty). Esto is 'this' when you're pointing at something without naming it.
Seco means 'dry'; mojado is 'wet'. If you name the item it changes to match: ¿La camiseta está seca?
¿Puedes + verb? = 'Can you...?' — a polite, everyday way to ask a favour. Lavar is 'to wash'; the washing machine is la lavadora.
Para mañana means 'for tomorrow'. Starting with esto puts the focus on the thing, like 'This — I need it for tomorrow.'
Sal comes from salir (to go out/leave). It's the short 'you do it' command, and sounds firm — add porfa (please) to soften it.
Cierra is the command from cerrar (to close). The opposite is abre la puerta, 'open the door'.
Entra means 'come in', but 'don't come in' changes the ending: no entres. 'Don't' commands in Spanish swap the a for an e like this.
Cambiarse (with the me) means changing your clothes. Without me, cambiar just means 'to change' something else.
El baño is the bathroom and also the everyday word for 'toilet' in Spain. Alguien means 'someone'.

phrases.en: Are you going to be long in the bathroom?
phrases.ph: teh KEH-dah MOO-choh ehn ehl BAH-nyoh
phrases.note: Literally 'Do you have much left in the bathroom?' ¿Te queda mucho? is a handy, polite way to ask 'Will you be long?'
In Spanish the describing word comes after: agua caliente is 'water hot'. Cold water is agua fría.
El secador comes from secar, 'to dry'. Hair straighteners are la plancha — the same word as a clothes iron.
Se ha acabado means 'it's run out' or 'it's finished'. With more than one thing: se han acabado las toallitas.
Papel higiénico is literally 'hygienic paper'. The h is silent and the g sounds like a throaty h.

phrases.en: Does this look OK on me?
phrases.note: Quedar bien is how Spanish says clothes suit or fit you. Te queda genial means 'it looks great on you'.
Ponerse means 'to put on' clothes, so this is 'I have nothing to put on'. Classic line in front of a full wardrobe.
Listo matches desayuno, which is a masculine ('el') word, so it doesn't change whoever is eating. Desayunar = 'to have breakfast'.
Lista ends in -a to match la comida, not the person. In Spain lunch (la comida) is the main meal, often around 2pm.
La cena is the evening meal, and cenar means 'to have dinner'. In Spain the c in cena sounds like 'th'.
It's the same words as 'Lunch is ready', because la comida means both 'food' and 'lunch'. Everyone will know what you mean.
Ven a + verb = 'Come and...' (ven is the command form of venir). Compare ve a: 'Go and...'.
A por means 'to fetch' and is very Spain-only. Ir a por = 'go and get': voy a por pan = 'I'm going to get bread'.

phrases.en: What do you want for breakfast?
phrases.note: Spanish has a verb that means 'to have breakfast', desayunar, so it's literally 'What do you want to breakfast?'

phrases.en: What do you want for lunch?
phrases.note: Comer means 'to eat', but in Spain it also means 'to have lunch'. For dinner, swap in cenar: ¿Qué quieres cenar?
Spanish says 'Do you have hunger?' using tener, not estar. The same goes for sed (thirst), frío (cold) and sueño (sleepiness).

phrases.en: Do you want something to eat?
phrases.note: Algo de comer = 'something to eat'. Note it's de, not para. Algo on its own means 'something' or 'anything'.
Literally 'something to drink'. It follows the same pattern as algo de comer. People also say ¿Quieres tomar algo?

phrases.en: What do you want to drink?
phrases.note: ¿Qué quieres + verb? = 'What do you want to...?' Beber has two b sounds, and they're softer than an English b.
There's no word for 'some' here. Spanish just says 'Do you want water?' Agua is feminine but takes el: el agua fría.
Más (with an accent) means 'more'. Handy answers: sí, un poco más (yes, a bit more) or no, gracias, estoy llena/lleno (I'm full).
Suficiente looks like 'sufficient' but is an everyday word. Bastante means the same and is just as common. The c is a 'th' sound in Spain.
Has + -ado word = 'Have you ...ed?' (terminar = to finish). The h in has is silent.
Comerse (with -te) means 'eat it all up', so it's stronger than just come. It sounds like a firm parent order.
Por lo menos = 'at least'. Pruébalo is 'try it', from probar (to try or taste), with lo ('it') stuck on the end.
Solo = 'just' or 'only', and un poco = 'a bit'. Prueba is the command form of probar, which is also used for trying on clothes.
Ni siquiera = 'not even'. It replaces no, so you don't need both. Lo ('it') goes before has.
For 'don't' orders the verb changes: come (eat!) becomes no comas (don't eat!). The h in ahora is silent.
Casi ('nearly') goes just before the word it describes. Lista ends in -a because la cena is feminine.

phrases.en: It'll be ready in ten minutes.
phrases.note: Estará = 'it will be' (the future of estar). Listo is for a masculine thing; if it's la cena, say lista. Diez ends in a 'th' sound.

phrases.en: Put your plate in the dishwasher.
phrases.es: Pon tu plato en el lavavajillas.
phrases.ph: pohn too PLAH-toh ehn ehl lah-bah-bah-HEE-yahs
phrases.note: Lavavajillas is 'washes-dishes' squashed into one word. Pon is the command form of poner (to put).
La basura means 'rubbish', but people also use it for the bin. Tíralo a la basura ('throw it in the bin') is just as common.

phrases.en: Put it back in the fridge.
phrases.es: Vuelve a ponerlo en la nevera.
phrases.ph: BWEHL-beh ah poh-NEHR-loh ehn lah neh-BEH-rah
phrases.note: Volver a + verb = 'to do something again', so here it's 'put it back'. La nevera is the usual word for the fridge in Spain.
¿Puedes + verb? = 'Can you...?', a polite everyday way to ask. To set the table, Spanish 'puts' it: poner la mesa.
It's the opposite of poner la mesa: quitar means 'to take away', so quitar la mesa = 'clear the table'. Recoger la mesa is also common.
Vaciar = 'to empty' (vacío means 'empty'). In Spain the c in vaciar is said like the 'th' in 'think'.
Cargar means 'to load'. It's the same verb as charging a phone (cargar el móvil). Vaciar is the opposite: 'to empty'.
Dejar means 'to leave (something somewhere)'. It's not salir, which is leaving a place. Esto = 'this' (a thing you don't name).

phrases.ph: kyehn seh ah koh-MEE-doh ehl OOL-tee-moh
phrases.note: Comerse means 'to scoff the lot', so it's perfect for accusations! Use la última if the thing is feminine, like la galleta.
Ahí means 'there' (near you), and allí is further away. Dejar becomes dejes after no, the 'don't' form.

phrases.en: Wash your hands before you eat.
phrases.es: Lávate las manos antes de comer.
phrases.ph: LAH-bah-teh lahs MAH-nohs AHN-tehs deh koh-MEHR
phrases.note: Lavarse las manos = 'to wash your hands'. Mano ends in -o but is feminine: la mano, las manos.
Siéntate comes from sentarse, 'to sit (yourself) down'. Adding por favor softens the order nicely.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.note: In Spain a request is often just a question in the present: 'Do you pass me the salt?' It sounds friendly, not rude.
Quema means 'it burns'. Caliente is 'hot' too, but que quema is the warning people actually shout. Here que just means 'because'.
Que aproveche is said when someone starts eating, like 'bon appétit'. It comes from aprovechar, 'to make the most of'.

phrases.en: Don't eat with your mouth open.
phrases.es: No comas con la boca abierta.
phrases.ph: noh KOH-mahs kohn lah BOH-kah ah-BYEHR-tah
phrases.note: Abierta ('open') ends in -a to match la boca. It's a classic parent line, so expect an eye roll.

phrases.es: Nada de móviles en la mesa.
phrases.ph: NAH-dah deh MOH-bee-lehs ehn lah MEH-sah
phrases.note: Nada de + thing = 'No... allowed'. It's handy for house rules: nada de chucherías (no sweets), nada de tele.
Quedar here means 'to be left'. It's just two words: ¿Queda leche? For plurals, add -n: ¿Quedan huevos?
Ayudar a + verb = 'help to...'. Don't forget the a. Cocinar = 'to cook' and la cocina = 'the kitchen'.
Gustar works backwards: 'Has it pleased you?' So it's ¿Te ha gustado?, and for plural things ¿Te han gustado?
Hay (said like 'eye') means 'there is'. Cenar is a verb, 'to have dinner', so this is literally 'What is there to have dinner?'
Literally 'When do we have dinner?' Spanish often uses the verb cenar instead of the noun. Swap in ¿A qué hora...? to ask 'At what time...?'
Lista matches la cena, which is a feminine ('la') word. For a masculine word it changes: ¿Está listo el desayuno? (Is breakfast ready?)
Vamos a + verb = 'we're going to...'. Handy pattern: vamos a ver (we'll see), vamos a salir (we're going out).
Spanish says 'I have hunger' — tengo means 'I have'. Same trick for tengo sed (I'm thirsty) and tengo frío (I'm cold). The h in hambre is silent.
Literally 'I'm dying of hunger'. Me muero de... works for any drama: me muero de sueño (I'm dead tired), me muero de vergüenza (I'm so embarrassed).
Algo means 'something' or 'anything'. Swap comer for beber to get ¿Hay algo de beber? — 'Is there anything to drink?'

phrases.en: Can I have something to eat?
phrases.note: ¿Puedo + verb? = 'Can I...?' — one of the most useful patterns there is: ¿Puedo salir?, ¿Puedo ver la tele?
Picar literally means 'to peck', and in Spain picar algo is the everyday way to say 'have a nibble or snack'.
Más means 'more' — the accent on the a is important, as mas without it means 'but'. For seconds at the table, Spanish families also say ¿Puedo repetir?

phrases.ph: meh PWEH-dehs ah-THEHR AHL-goh deh koh-MEHR
phrases.note: Me at the start means 'for me'. Hacer means both 'to make' and 'to do', so de comer ('to eat') makes it clear you mean food.
¿Podemos...? is 'Can we...?' — the 'we' version of ¿Puedo...? Pizza keeps its Italian 'ts' sound, not a Spanish th.
Pedir means 'to order' or 'to ask for', so this is 'Can we order food?' There's no single everyday word for 'takeaway' — comida a domicilio is home delivery.
Al is a + el squashed together, meaning 'to the'. It always happens: ir al cine, ir al parque, ir al McDonald's.
Gustar works backwards: literally 'That doesn't please me'. For more than one thing it becomes gustan — no me gustan las setas (I don't like mushrooms).
Quiero is 'I want', from querer. It can sound blunt on its own — adding gracias (No quiero eso, gracias) keeps it polite.
Just put no in front of the verb to make it negative: tengo hambre becomes no tengo hambre. No 'do/don't' needed in Spanish.
Ya means 'already'. He comido is 'I have eaten' — he + a verb ending in -ido/-ado, just like 'I have' + 'eaten' in English.
The -é ending on comeré means 'I will'. Luego is the everyday word for 'later' — you'll also hear hasta luego, 'see you later'.

phrases.en: Can I eat in my room?
phrases.note: Habitación is 'bedroom' — the h is silent and the stress falls on the final -ción. You'll also hear mi cuarto.
Aperitivos are nibbles like crisps, nuts and olives. Están (not son) is used because you're asking where things are — location always uses estar.
Watch out: patatas fritas means both crisps and chips. If it's unclear, say patatas fritas de bolsa ('from a bag') for crisps.
No word for 'any' needed — ¿Hay...? covers 'Is there any...?' Chocolate has four syllables in Spanish, stressed on the -la-.

phrases.ph: kyehn seh ah koh-MEE-doh mee koh-MEE-dah
phrases.note: The se in se ha comido adds a sense of 'ate it all up'. Comer (to eat) and comida (food) come from the same word.
Guardar means 'to keep' or 'to save'. Me lo estaba guardando is 'I was keeping it for myself' — perfect when your brother's eaten your leftovers.
Beber is 'to drink'. Remember b and v sound the same in Spanish, so beber has two soft b sounds.

phrases.en: Can you get me some water?
phrases.note: Traer means 'to bring'. Agua is feminine but says el agua, not la agua — it's an exception because it starts with a stressed a.
Rico usually means 'rich', but with food it means 'tasty'. Está muy rico is the go-to compliment for someone's cooking.
Llena means 'full' and is for a girl — a boy says estoy lleno. The double l sounds like an English y.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.note: Pasar means 'to pass'. ¿Me pasas...? works for anything at the table: ¿Me pasas el agua?, ¿Me pasas el pan?
No queda means 'there's none left', from quedar (to remain). Swap the food: no queda pan, no quedan galletas.
Una tostada is a slice of toast. The me on hacerme means 'for myself' — 'Can I make myself some toast?'
Demasiado means 'too (much)'. Caliente is for hot food and drinks — for hot weather Spanish says hace calor instead.
Literally 'Do I help you cook?' — Spanish often offers help this way. Ayudar a + verb = 'help to do something'.
Buenísimo is bueno ('good') turned up to max with -ísimo. Try it with other words: riquísimo, carísimo (so expensive).
Siéntate is 'sit yourself down', from sentarse. Bien (well) does the job of 'properly' here.

phrases.es: Quita los codos de la mesa.
phrases.ph: KEE-tah lohs KOH-dohs deh lah MEH-sah
phrases.note: Quita means 'take off/remove' and codos are elbows. Quitar is a really useful verb: quita eso = move that.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.es: No hables con la boca llena.
phrases.ph: noh AH-blehs kohn lah BOH-kah YEH-nah
phrases.note: Llena means full; boca is mouth. In Spain ll sounds like the English y in 'yes'.

phrases.es: Usa el cuchillo y el tenedor.
phrases.ph: OO-sah ehl koo-CHEE-yoh ee ehl teh-neh-DOHR
phrases.note: Cuchillo is knife and tenedor is fork. A spoon is una cuchara — easy to mix up with cuchillo.
Lo del plato means 'what's on the plate'. The -te on termínate adds a sense of 'finish it all up yourself'.
Rico means 'rich' but for food it means tasty. Use está for how food tastes right now.
Quién is 'who'. Más means 'more' — the accent stops it being mas, an old word for 'but'.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the bread?
phrases.note: Spanish often asks 'do you pass me...?' instead of 'can you pass me...?'. It sounds friendly, not rude.
Deja de + verb = 'stop doing'. Deja de cantar, deja de hablar, deja de molestar.
¿Quieres más? = 'do you want more?'. Add de + food: ¿Quieres más de pasta?
Has terminado = 'have you finished'. Spain uses this 'has + -ado' form for things that just happened.
Espera a que = 'wait until'. Todos = everyone; it goes after the verb here, which sounds natural.
Tenedor = fork, cuchillo = knife, cuchara = spoon. Spanish says 'the fork', not 'your fork'.
Verdura = veg, usually singular in Spain. Cómete (not just come) means 'eat it all up'.
Fuera = 'out' / 'away'. Móvil is the Spain word for mobile phone. Short and bossy.

phrases.es: Deja de jugar con la comida.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh hoo-GAHR kohn lah koh-MEE-dah
phrases.note: Jugar con = to play with. Comida means 'food' and also 'lunch' in Spain.
Quisquillosa = fussy, picky. It's for a girl — a boy is quisquilloso.
No le pasa nada = 'nothing's wrong with it'. Also used for people: ¿Qué te pasa? = what's wrong?
Quejarse = to moan or complain. No te quejes = don't moan. Very common parent line.
Classic parent sarcasm. Add: ¡No hay carta! = 'there's no menu!'.
Quieta = still, not moving. It's for a girl — say estate quieto to a boy.

phrases.es: Deja de darle patadas a tu hermano.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh DAHR-leh pah-TAH-dahs ah too ehr-MAH-noh
phrases.note: Dar patadas = to kick (literally 'give kicks'). Le points to tu hermano.

phrases.en: Don't feed Monty under the table.
phrases.es: No le des de comer a Monty por debajo de la mesa.
phrases.ph: noh leh dehs deh koh-MEHR ah MOHN-tee pohr deh-BAH-hoh deh lah MEH-sah
phrases.note: Dar de comer = to feed. Por debajo de = underneath. Monty will be very disappointed.
Masticar = to chew. Boca cerrada = closed mouth — cerrada matches boca, which is feminine.
Límpiate = 'wipe yourself'. The -te on the end means you do it to yourself. Servilleta = napkin.

phrases.en: Say thank you for the food.
phrases.es: Da las gracias por la comida.
phrases.ph: dah lahs GRAH-thyahs pohr lah koh-MEE-dah
phrases.note: Dar las gracias = to say thank you. Por = 'for' when you thank someone.
Estirarse = to stretch across. Pídelo = 'ask for it' — the lo on the end means 'it'.
Recoger = to clear away or tidy up. Recoger la mesa = to clear the table.
Bueno means good, and -ísimo turns it into 'super good'. Stays buenísimo because it describes the food, not you.
Literally 'can I get up from the table?'. ¿Puedo + verb? = 'Can I...?' — one of the most useful patterns there is.
Picar means 'to sting' or 'to be spicy', so this is 'it stings a lot'. Spicy food is comida picante.
Postre is dessert or pudding. Hay (sounds like 'eye') means 'is there' or 'are there'.

phrases.en: Can I have a bit less?
phrases.note: Poner means 'to put', so it's 'will you put me a bit less?' — how Spanish people ask for a portion. Swap menos for más to get more.
Spanish says 'this doesn't please me': no me gusta. For more than one thing: no me gustan.
Odio = 'I hate'. Strong but normal about food: odio las coles de Bruselas.
Asqueroso = disgusting. Use está for how food tastes. Rude to the cook — careful!
¡Qué asco! = 'how gross!'. Asco means disgust. Use qué + word for 'how...!': ¡qué rico!

phrases.en: Why do we keep having this?
phrases.ph: pohr keh SYEHM-preh koh-MEH-mohs loh MEES-moh
phrases.note: Lo mismo = 'the same thing'. Siempre = always. A natural way to moan about repeats.
Otra vez = 'again' (literally 'another time'). Put no at the end for extra drama.
¿Puedo...? = 'can I...?'. More casual: ¿Me pones más? = 'will you give me more?'.
Llena = full — it's for a girl; a boy says lleno. Also: no puedo más = 'I can't eat any more'.
¿Me puedo ir? = 'can I go?'. Irse means to leave — the me shows it's you who's leaving.
Frío = cold. Food that's gone cold uses estar. Lukewarm is tibio.
¿Qué es esto? = 'what's this?'. Said with a face, it's a complaint, not a question.
¡Qué rico! = 'yummy!'. In Spain rico means tasty when talking about food (it also means rich).
¿Me pasas...? = 'can you pass me...?'. Swap in anything: la sal, el agua, el pan.
Dile que = 'tell him to'. Pare comes from parar (to stop). Aimed at your brother.
Copiar = to copy. Está + -ando = 'is doing right now'. The ultimate sibling complaint.
Más que = 'more than'. Pair it with ¡No es justo! = 'it's not fair!'.
Justo = fair. You can also use justo to mean 'just' or 'exactly': justo ahora.
Vegetariana is for a girl — a boy says vegetariano. Soy is used for what you are, not how you feel.

phrases.en: Do I have to eat all of it?
phrases.ph: meh loh TEHN-goh keh koh-MEHR TOH-doh
phrases.note: Tener que = to have to. Me lo... todo = 'all of it'. Classic bargaining line.
Poquito = 'a tiny bit'. Adding -ito makes things small (or cute): un momentito.
Postre = pudding or dessert. De postre = 'for pudding'; de primero = for the first course.

phrases.en: Can I have it with nothing on it?
phrases.note: Sin nada = 'with nothing' / plain. Sin means 'without': sin salsa, sin cebolla.
¿Qué tal + thing? = 'How was/is...?', with no verb needed. In Spain secondary school is el instituto (or el insti for short).
Día ends in -a but is masculine, so it's el día. That's a classic GCSE trap. ¿Qué tal? on its own means 'How's it going?'
Hecho = 'done/made', from hacer. With hoy (today), Spain uses has hecho ('have you done'). Both h's are silent.
Pasar means 'to happen' as well as 'to pass'. ¿Qué ha pasado? = 'What's happened?' The describing word goes after algo.
In Spain homework is los deberes, which is always plural. It literally means 'duties'.
Hacer los deberes = 'to do homework'. Hecho is the odd 'done' form of hacer, so learn it by heart.
Literally 'For when is it?' Para cuándo is the natural way to ask about a deadline. Answer with es para el lunes (it's for Monday).
Lo = 'it', and it goes before has, not after terminado. If 'it' is something feminine, like la redacción, say la has terminado.
No word for 'any' is needed: Spanish just asks 'Do you need help?' Necesitar = 'to need', and ayuda = 'help'.

phrases.en: Have you got a test tomorrow?
phrases.note: Examen covers both tests and exams. Mañana means 'tomorrow', but la mañana is 'the morning'.
Spanish just says estudiar ('to study') for revising. Revisar actually means 'to check', so don't use it for revising.

phrases.en: What lesson have you got first?
phrases.note: A lesson is una clase, and 'I've got maths' is tengo mates. Lección is more like a chapter in a textbook.
To answer, use a las + time: termino a las tres y media ('I finish at half three'). Salgo a las... ('I get out at...') works too.
Literally 'Do I have to pick you up?' Recoger is the Spain word for collecting someone, and te ('you') is stuck on the end.

phrases.en: Where should I pick you up?
phrases.note: Spanish uses the plain present, 'Where do I pick you up?', to ask this. Recoger changes g to j in recojo to keep the h sound.

phrases.en: What time should I pick you up?
phrases.note: It's the same trick as ¿Dónde te recojo?: the simple present works for 'should I'. For example, ¿Te llevo? = 'Shall I take you?'
Escribir ('to write') is how people say 'to text' or 'message'. After cuando about the future, terminas changes to termines.

phrases.en: Let me know when you're ready.
phrases.note: Avisar = 'to let someone know'. Lista is for a girl, so tell a boy cuando estés listo.

phrases.es: No te olvides de la ropa de deporte.
phrases.ph: noh teh ohl-BEE-dehs deh lah RROH-pah deh deh-POHR-teh
phrases.note: There's no single word for 'PE kit', so it's la ropa de deporte ('sports clothes'). PE itself is educación física, or just edu.
Spanish 'prepares' a bag: preparar la mochila. For a suitcase, people say hacer la maleta.

phrases.en: Do you need anything for tomorrow?
phrases.note: In questions algo means 'anything', and in answers it means 'something'. Para mañana = 'for tomorrow'.
Haz is the short command form of hacer ('do!'). In Spain the z at the end is said like the 'th' in 'bath'.

phrases.en: What have you got to do?
phrases.note: Tener que + verb = 'to have to'. Note the two different words that sound like ke: qué (what) and que (to).

phrases.es: ¿Qué tal te ha ido el examen?
phrases.ph: keh tahl teh ah EE-doh ehl ehk-SAH-mehn
phrases.note: Literally 'How has the exam gone for you?' Ido is 'gone', from ir. A quick reply is me ha ido bien or mal.
In Spain you 'take out' a mark: sacar una nota. He sacado un ocho = 'I got an 8' (marks there go out of 10).
Bien hecho is literally 'well done'. For extra praise try ¡Muy bien! or ¡Qué bien!

phrases.en: Who did you have lunch with?
phrases.note: In Spanish con ('with') has to go at the start of the question, never at the end like in English.
Amigas is for friends who are all girls. If any boys are in the group, it becomes amigos.
Enseñar means both 'to show' and 'to teach'. Lo que = 'what' in the middle of a sentence (not qué).

phrases.en: Put your books in your bag.
phrases.es: Mete los libros en la mochila.
phrases.ph: MEH-teh lohs LEE-brohs ehn lah moh-CHEE-lah
phrases.note: Meter means 'to put in'. Use it instead of poner when something goes inside something else. Watch out: libro means 'book', not library (biblioteca).

phrases.en: Don't leave it till the last minute.
phrases.es: No lo dejes para el último momento.
phrases.ph: noh loh DEH-hehs PAH-rah ehl OOL-tee-moh moh-MEHN-toh
phrases.note: Dejar para = 'to leave for (later)'. Spanish says 'last moment' (último momento) rather than 'last minute'.
Los deberes is 'homework' in Spain — it's plural, and literally means 'duties'. No word for 'any' is needed.
Hecho is the irregular 'done' form of hacer. Both h's are silent. Lo (it) goes before he, not after.
Haré means 'I will do'. It's the classic teenager reply — a parent might answer ¡No, ahora! (No, now!).

phrases.en: I need help with my homework.
phrases.note: Necesito means 'I need' and works with a thing or a verb: necesito ayuda (I need help), necesito estudiar (I need to study).

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Ayudarme is ayudar (to help) + me glued on the end. You could also say ¿Me ayudas con esto? — just as common.
Entender (to understand) changes its e to ie in entiendo. Great for class too: No lo entiendo — 'I don't get it'.
Mirar means 'to look at', so this is 'Can you have a look at this?' For checking carefully, revisar is the word.
Tengo que + verb = 'I have to...'. Really useful: tengo que irme (I have to go), tengo que estudiar.
La impresora is 'the printer', from imprimir (to print). No funciona works for any gadget that's broken or playing up.

phrases.en: I need something for school tomorrow.
phrases.es: Necesito algo para el instituto mañana.
phrases.ph: neh-theh-SEE-toh AHL-goh PAH-rah ehl eens-tee-TOO-toh mah-NYAH-nah
phrases.note: Mañana means 'tomorrow', but la mañana means 'the morning' — so mañana por la mañana is 'tomorrow morning'.
Literally 'it forgot itself on me' — a sneaky way of saying it's not really your fault! Olvidar means 'to forget'.
Dinero is 'money'. Para means 'for' here, as in 'for a purpose' — para la excursión, para el comedor (school canteen).

phrases.en: I need you to sign this.
phrases.note: Firmar is 'to sign'. After necesito que ('I need you to'), the verb changes its ending from firmas to firmes.
Un examen covers tests and exams. The x sounds like 'ks'. The plural gains an accent: exámenes.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.note: No quiero + verb = 'I don't want to...'. Ir is 'to go', and al is a + el ('to the').
Cansada is for a girl — a boy says cansado. Uses estar (estoy) because tiredness is how you feel right now.
Aburrido means 'boring' with ser, but 'bored' with estar: estoy aburrida (I'm bored — a boy says aburrido). Ha sido is 'it has been'.
A casual, clipped reply — no verb needed, just like saying 'School? Fine.' The perfect answer to ¿Qué tal el instituto?
Spanish uses a double negative: no... nada = 'not... nothing'. That's correct in Spanish, not a mistake.
Sé with an accent means 'I know' (from saber). Without the accent, se is a different little word — so the accent matters when writing.
Acordarse means 'to remember', and the o changes to ue in acuerdo. Add de for what you can't remember: no me acuerdo de su nombre.
Hemos is 'we have', so hemos hecho is 'we have done'. Nada means 'nothing', and pairs with no in a double negative.
Recoger means 'to pick up' or 'collect' — it's also the word for tidying up. The g before e sounds like a throaty h.

phrases.en: Can you pick me up early?
phrases.note: Antes means 'before' or 'earlier'. Its opposite is después (later/after), so you could also ask ¿Puedes recogerme después?

phrases.en: What time are you picking me up?
phrases.note: ¿A qué hora...? = 'At what time...?' — reuse it for anything: ¿A qué hora cenamos? The present recoges works for future plans too.
A very Spanish phrase: tomar la lección means asking someone questions to check they've learnt it. Perfect before a test.
Literally 'It's for tomorrow'. Para + a day is how Spanish says when something is due: es para el lunes.
Sacar literally means 'to take out', but sacar una nota means 'to get a mark'. Sacar un diez is top marks in Spain.
Aprobar means 'to pass' a test or subject. Students celebrate with ¡He aprobado todo! when they've passed everything.
Suspender looks like 'suspend', but at school it means 'to fail'. A failed mark is called un suspenso.
Spanish uses estudiar (to study) for revising. Don't use revisar — that means 'to check' something.
In Spain a computer is el ordenador (from ordenar, 'to put in order'). Latin America says la computadora.
Literally 'They've punished me'. Castigar is 'to punish' and covers detentions — and being grounded at home.
Una excursión is a school trip or day out — not just a hike. You'll often need money and a signed form for one!
Ve comes from ir (to go), so ve a + verb means 'go and...'. Ordenar is 'to tidy' — it's related to 'order', putting things in order.

phrases.es: Tu habitación está hecha un desastre.
phrases.ph: too ah-bee-tah-THYOHN ehs-TAH EH-chah oon deh-SAHS-treh
phrases.note: Literally 'your room is made into a disaster'. Hecha matches habitación (a 'feminine' word) — you'd say hecho for a masculine one, like el salón.
Has + ordenado works just like English 'have + tidied'. Swap in other -ado words: ¿Has limpiado...? (cleaned), ¿Has terminado? (finished).
Recoger means 'to pick up' or 'to clear up'. Recoge tu habitación is another common way to say 'tidy your room'.
Guardar means 'to put away' or 'keep safe' — it's where the English word 'guard' comes from. No separate word for 'away' is needed.
Ropa means 'clothes' but it's a singular word — tu ropa, not tus ropas. Think of it like 'clothing'.

phrases.en: Put your dirty clothes in the wash.
phrases.es: Pon la ropa sucia para lavar.
phrases.ph: pohn lah RROH-pah SOO-thyah PAH-rah lah-BAHR
phrases.note: Literally 'put the dirty clothes for washing'. Pon is the short command from poner (to put) — one of the handiest words around the house.
Limpio = clean, sucio = dirty. They use está (not es) because being clean or dirty can change. Talking about a shirt (la camiseta)? Say limpia o sucia.

phrases.en: Don't leave it on the floor.
phrases.es: No lo dejes en el suelo.
phrases.ph: noh loh DEH-hehs ehn ehl SWEH-loh
phrases.note: Dejar is 'to leave', but 'don't...' changes it to no dejes. El suelo is the floor you walk on — not a 'floor' (storey) of a building, which is la planta.
Haz is the short command from hacer (to make/do). Spanish says 'make the bed' rather than 'your bed' — it's obvious whose bed it is.
Abre comes from abrir (to open). Blinds are las persianas — very common in Spain, so you'll hear sube la persiana ('put the blind up') a lot.
La ventana is a window in a house. Careful: the window of a car or a ticket office is la ventanilla.
Cierra comes from cerrar (to close). The e changes to ie in the stressed part — so it's cierra, not cerra.
Spanish doesn't split 'shut' and 'close' — cerrar covers both. Add ya on the end (Cierra la puerta ya) if you mean 'right now'.
Abierta ('open') ends in -a to match la puerta. For a window left shut you'd say Deja la ventana cerrada.
Apagar means 'to switch off' — use it for lights, the TV, your phone or the oven. In Spain the z in luz sounds like 'th'.
Encender ('to switch on') is the opposite of apagar. It also means 'to light', like lighting a candle or the fire.
Bajar means 'to go down' or 'bring down', so one word does the job of 'bring downstairs'. Useful pattern: ¿Puedes + verb? = 'Can you...?'
Subir ('to go up / take up') is the partner of bajar. Esto means 'this' (near me); eso means 'that' (near you).

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Ayudar is 'to help'; the -me stuck on the end means 'me'. So ayudarme = 'to help me' — all one word.
Literally 'throw me a hand' — echar means 'to throw'. Mano is feminine even though it ends in -o, so it's una mano.
Spanish has no word for 'whose' — you say 'of whom is this?'. Answer with Es de... : Es de mi hermano (It's my brother's).
Tuyo = 'yours'. It becomes tuya if the thing is feminine, e.g. ¿Esta sudadera es tuya? (Is this hoodie yours?).
Va is from ir (to go), so it's word for word 'where goes this?'. Spanish often puts the thing at the end of a question like this.

phrases.es: ¿Puedes pasar la aspiradora por tu habitación?
phrases.ph: PWEH-dehs pah-SAHR lah ahs-pee-rah-DOH-rah pohr too ah-bee-tah-THYOHN
phrases.note: Spanish 'passes the vacuum cleaner' round a room: pasar la aspiradora. Aspirar means 'to suck in'.
Las sábanas are sheets — the accent shows the stress goes on the first syllable. A duvet is el edredón and a pillow is la almohada.
Cuelga comes from colgar (to hang) — o becomes ue. Colgar also means 'to hang up' the phone.
Sacar = 'to take out'. La basura means both 'rubbish' and 'the bin', so this is literally 'take out the rubbish'.

phrases.en: Can you hang the washing out?
phrases.note: Tender means 'to spread out / hang out' — used just for washing. The clothes airer or line is el tendedero.
Literally 'take the clothes off the washing line'. Quitar = 'to take off / remove'.
Doblar means 'to fold' — and also 'to turn' a corner, and 'to dub' a film (una película doblada).
Huele comes from oler (to smell) — a strange one that adds an h. Huele mal = smells bad; huele bien = smells nice.

phrases.en: There are dirty cups in your room.
phrases.es: Hay tazas sucias en tu habitación.
phrases.ph: eye TAH-thahs SOO-thyahs ehn too ah-bee-tah-THYOHN
phrases.note: Hay (said like 'eye') means 'there is' or 'there are'. Sucias ends in -as to match tazas (cups).
Tocar here means 'to be someone's turn': me toca = it's my turn, le toca = it's his turn. The a mí adds 'ME, not someone else'.
Hice = 'I did', from hacer. It's irregular, so learn it on its own: hice, hiciste, hizo.
Habitación is the everyday word for bedroom in Spain. Está bien = 'it's fine' — use estar for how something is right now.

phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh ehn-TRAHR ehn mee ah-bee-tah-THYOHN
phrases.note: Deja de + verb = 'stop doing something'. Handy pattern: deja de gritar, deja de cantar.
Mis cosas = 'my stuff' — cosas (things) is how Spanish says stuff. No toques = 'don't touch' when talking to one person.
Spanish often uses the present for the near future: lo hago = 'I'll do it'. Después de esto = 'after this'.

phrases.es: ¿Por qué siempre me toca a mí?
phrases.ph: pohr keh SYEHM-preh meh TOH-kah ah mee
phrases.note: Literally 'why is it always my turn?'. Siempre (always) goes before the verb, unlike English.
La stands for la habitación, so it's la, not lo. Ya here means 'already' — it adds a 'see, done!' feel.
La aspiradora = the hoover. To hoover is pasar la aspiradora.

phrases.en: It's his turn to empty the dishwasher.
phrases.es: Le toca a él vaciar el lavavajillas.
phrases.ph: leh TOH-kah ah ehl bah-THYAHR ehl lah-bah-bah-HEE-yahs
phrases.note: Le toca a él + verb = 'it's his turn to…'. Lavavajillas = dishwasher, literally 'wash-dishes'.
Así = 'like this' or 'this way'. Short and very useful: hazlo así = do it like this.
Sé = 'I know' (a fact), from saber. Todo = everything. The classic messy-room defence.
Llamar means 'to call' but also 'to knock' at a door. Literally 'knock before coming in'.
The me means 'for me / on me' — like 'don't go tidying my room'. Spanish uses la (the) where English says 'my'.

phrases.en: Where did you put my hoodie?
phrases.note: Sudadera = hoodie or sweatshirt. Has puesto = 'have you put', from poner — puesto is irregular.
Spanish needs the double negative: no encuentro nada = 'I can't find anything', literally 'I don't find nothing'.
Ya voy = 'I'm coming' — Spanish says 'I'm going' where English says 'coming'. Vale is Spain's 'OK'.
Sucio = dirty; limpio = clean. Change the ending to match: la camiseta no está sucia.
Hacer la cama = to make the bed. Hecho is the irregular 'done/made' form of hacer.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do everything?
phrases.es: ¿Por qué tengo que hacerlo todo yo?
phrases.ph: pohr keh TEHN-goh keh ah-THEHR-loh TOH-doh yoh
phrases.note: Tengo que + verb = 'I have to…'. Putting yo at the end stresses 'ME' — very moany, very real.
Luego = 'later' — the teen's favourite word. Significa = 'means', like 'signify'.

phrases.en: I don't care whose it is.
phrases.es: Me da igual de quién sea.
phrases.ph: meh dah ee-GWAHL deh kyehn SEH-ah
phrases.note: Me da igual = 'I don't care' or 'it's all the same to me'. De quién = whose, literally 'of who'.
Sin = without. Excusas is an easy one — same as English. Poner excusas = to make excuses.

phrases.es: ¡A mí no me digas «me da igual»!
phrases.ph: ah mee noh meh DEE-gahs meh dah ee-GWAHL
phrases.note: Spanish teens say me da igual or paso for 'whatever'. A mí no me digas… = 'don't you say … to ME'.

phrases.en: Don't roll your eyes at me.
phrases.es: No me pongas los ojos en blanco.
phrases.ph: noh meh POHN-gahs lohs OH-hohs ehn BLAHN-koh
phrases.note: Poner los ojos en blanco = to roll your eyes, literally 'put your eyes in white'.
Literally 'because I say it'. Yo at the end stresses who's in charge. Porque (one word, no accent) = because.

phrases.en: You said that an hour ago.
phrases.note: Hace + time = 'ago': hace una hora = an hour ago, hace dos días = two days ago.

phrases.es: No te lo vuelvo a pedir.
phrases.ph: noh teh loh BWEHL-boh ah peh-DEER
phrases.note: Volver a + verb = 'to do something again'. No te lo vuelvo a decir = I'm not telling you again.
Contestar = to answer, but no me contestes means 'don't answer me back' — it's about the cheek.
Cuento = 'I count', from contar. Then comes the famous: uno… dos… (and hopefully never tres).
Putting no after the phrase is a natural way to say 'not X, Y'. Ahora = now; ahora mismo = right now.

phrases.en: You're not busy, you're on your phone.
phrases.es: No estás ocupada, estás con el móvil.
phrases.ph: noh ehs-TAHS oh-koo-PAH-dah, ehs-TAHS kohn ehl MOH-beel
phrases.note: Ocupada is for a girl — a boy is ocupado. Estar con el móvil = to be on your phone; móvil is Spain's word.

phrases.en: I don't care who did it.
phrases.es: Me da igual quién lo haya hecho.
phrases.ph: meh dah ee-GWAHL kyehn loh AH-yah EH-choh
phrases.note: Haya hecho = 'did / has done', a form Spanish uses after me da igual. Just learn the whole chunk.

phrases.en: If you know, why haven't you done it?
phrases.es: Si lo sabes, ¿por qué no lo has hecho?
phrases.ph: see loh SAH-behs, pohr keh noh loh ahs EH-choh
phrases.note: The comeback to ya lo sé (I know). Si without an accent = if; sí with one = yes.

phrases.ph: ehn-TOHN-thehs, pohr keh noh ehs-TAH EH-choh
phrases.note: Entonces = 'then' or 'so'. Está hecho = 'it's done'. Hecho is the 'done' form of hacer.
Intento = attempt, from intentar (to try). Buen is bueno with the o dropped before a masculine word.
Resoplar = to huff and puff, that loud annoyed breath. Deja de + verb = stop doing it.
Literally 'I already know that one'. Esa and la are feminine because they mean la excusa.
A set phrase for 'don't give me that' or 'don't come to me with those excuses'. Sounds firm but not rude.
Spanish says 'put' excuses: poner excusas. Deja de = stop.
Haré is 'I will do' (from hacer). The h is silent and the accent tells you to stress the end.

phrases.en: I'll do it in a minute.
phrases.note: Lo hago is 'I do it' — Spanish uses the present for things you're about to do. Teens in Spain also say ahora lo hago.

phrases.en: I was going to do it!
phrases.note: Iba a + verb = 'I was going to...'. The lo (it) is stuck on the end of hacer to make hacerlo.
Sé means 'I know' (from saber). Adding ya makes it 'I already know' — it can sound a bit fed up, just like in English.
Word by word: 'already me it you-have said'. Dicho is 'said', from decir. Flip it for a parent: ya te lo he dicho.
He oído = 'I have heard' — in Spain this form is used for things that just happened. The h in he is silent.
Estoy + a word ending in -ando/-iendo = 'I'm ...ing' right now. Haciendo is 'doing' — in Spain the c sounds like 'th'.
Espera is the 'you do it' form of esperar (to wait). On its own it can sound sharp — espera un momento is softer.
Literally 'wait a moment'. Spanish has no 'hang on' idiom, so this is the friendly way to ask for a bit of time.
Short and easy — un segundo is 'one second'. Un momento or un minuto work the same way.
Written as two words for 'why?'. The answer 'because' is one word: porque. They sound almost the same.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do it?
phrases.ph: pohr keh TEHN-goh keh ah-THEHR-loh yoh
phrases.note: Putting yo ('me') at the end adds a 'why me?' feeling. Without it, it's just a plain question.

phrases.ph: pohr keh noh PWEH-deh ah-THEHR-loh ehl
phrases.note: Él (with an accent) means 'he'; without the accent, el means 'the'. Putting él at the end points at your brother.
Mío = 'mine'. It changes with the thing: no es mía for a feminine word like la taza. The accent keeps the stress on the i.
Starting with yo stresses 'I didn't — someone else did'. He hecho = 'I have done'; both h's are silent.
Literally 'I haven't been'. Yo no he sido is the classic Spanish 'it wasn't me!' — every Spanish kid knows it.

phrases.es: Yo no lo he dejado ahí.
phrases.ph: yoh noh loh eh deh-HAH-doh ah-EE
phrases.note: Dejar means 'to leave' something somewhere. Ahí is 'there' (near you) — don't mix it up with hay (there is).
Ordenar means 'to tidy' (put in order) — not 'to order' food, which is pedir. Ordenador (computer) comes from the same word.

phrases.es: Mi habitación no está tan mal.
phrases.ph: mee ah-bee-tah-THYOHN noh ehs-TAH tahn mahl
phrases.note: Tan mal = 'that bad'. Use está (not es) because the mess is a state that can change... in theory.
Spanish just says 'I don't find it' — no word for 'can't' needed. Encontrar is 'to find'.
Va is 'goes' (from ir). Simple and useful when putting shopping or washing away.

phrases.en: What do you want me to do?
phrases.note: Quieres que... = 'you want (someone) to...'. After it, hago changes to haga — just learn this one as a set phrase.
English can stop at 'have to?', but Spanish needs the verb: hacerlo, 'do it'. Say it with a groan for full effect.
Hice means 'I did' (from hacer) — no accent and the h is silent. Ayer is 'yesterday'.
Tocar usually means 'to touch', but le toca = 'it's his turn'. Very common for chores and games.
Me toca = 'it's my turn'. Adding a mí on the end stresses 'not me!' Ask ¿A quién le toca? for 'Whose turn is it?'
Siempre = 'always'. The yo at the end adds 'it's always me' — a classic complaint.
Ocupada is for a girl — a boy says ocupado. Use estoy because being busy is temporary.
Terminar = 'to finish'. Ya adds 'already/done now'. Even shorter: ¡Ya está! ('That's it, done!').
Limpio = 'clean'; change to limpia for feminine things like la cocina. Here ya means 'now'.
Mañana means 'tomorrow' but also 'morning' — por la mañana is 'in the morning'.

phrases.en: What do I get for it?
phrases.ph: ee keh meh dahs ah KAHM-byoh
phrases.note: A cambio means 'in return' (cambio = 'change/exchange'). Starting with y ('and') makes it sound cheeky.
Culpa = 'fault' or 'blame'. Mía goes after it and ends in -a to match culpa.
In Spain a mobile is el móvil — el teléfono sounds more like the landline. Deja literally means 'leave', as in 'leave it alone'.
Adding ya ('already') makes it impatient — like 'put it down, already!'. It sounds firmer than plain Deja el móvil.

phrases.en: How long have you been on your phone?
phrases.ph: KWAHN-toh TYEHM-poh YEH-bahs kohn ehl MOH-beel
phrases.note: Llevar usually means 'to carry', but ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas...? is the Spanish way to ask 'how long have you been...?'. Reply: Llevo diez minutos.
Baja ('lower it') is the go-to word for turning the volume down. The opposite is sube la música — 'turn it up'.
Baja + lo ('it') joined into one word. The accent on á keeps the stress in the same place once the extra bit is added.
Alto means 'high' or 'tall', and for sound it means 'loud'. Demasiado = 'too (much)'. 'Too quiet' is demasiado bajo.
Ponte means 'put on (yourself)' — the same word for clothes: ponte el abrigo. Headphones are los auriculares, or los cascos for big ones.
La tele is the everyday word for the TV, just like 'the telly'. Baja here means 'turn down the volume', not 'take it downstairs'!
Estás + viendo = 'are watching' — viendo comes from ver (to see/watch). Spanish uses ver for watching TV, not mirar.
Jugar (to play a game) needs a: you play 'at' something — juego al Minecraft. Don't miss the a at the start of the question.
Literally 'with whom do you talk?'. Spanish can't end a question on 'to' or 'with' — con goes at the front. The h in hablas is silent.
Sigues comes from seguir (to carry on), and it's how Spanish says 'still': ¿Sigues en la cama? = 'Are you still in bed?'
Literally 'you have to charge the phone'. Tienes que + verb = 'you have to...' — a pattern you'll use all day.
El cargador (charger) comes from cargar (to charge) — -dor on the end often means 'the thing that does it'.

phrases.en: Don't forget to charge your phone.
phrases.es: No te olvides de cargar el móvil.
phrases.ph: noh teh ohl-BEE-dehs deh kahr-GAHR ehl MOH-beel
phrases.note: No te olvides de... = 'Don't forget to...'. Remember the de before the next verb — no te olvides de llamar (don't forget to call).
La pantalla is 'the screen', and Spanish just says 'enough screen' for screen time. Bastante = 'enough'.
Es hora de + verb = 'it's time to...'. Dejarlo means 'to leave it', so this is 'time to leave it' — Spanish has no 'come off'.

phrases.es: Cinco minutos más y lo dejas.
phrases.ph: THEEN-koh mee-NOO-tohs mahs ee loh DEH-hahs
phrases.note: Más goes after the number: cinco minutos más ('five minutes more'). In Spain cinco starts with a 'th' sound.

phrases.en: No, I'm not extending your time limit.
phrases.es: No, no voy a darte más tiempo.
phrases.ph: noh, noh boy ah DAHR-teh mahs TYEHM-poh
phrases.note: Literally 'No, I'm not going to give you more time'. The double no is normal — the first answers, the second makes the sentence negative.

phrases.en: Why do you need more time?
phrases.note: ¿Por qué? (two words) = 'why?'; porque (one word) = 'because'. Tiempo means both 'time' and 'weather'.
Literally 'rest your sight'. La vista means 'eyesight' — Spanish talks about resting la vista rather than los ojos (the eyes).
Apaga = 'switch off'. The same word works for the light, your phone or the computer: apaga el ordenador.
El mando is the TV remote in Spain (short for mando a distancia). It's also the word for a games controller.
Escribir is 'to write', and it's the normal word for texting too. Spaniards also say mandar un wasap (send a WhatsApp).
El ordenador is 'computer' in Spain (Latin America says la computadora). A laptop is un portátil.

phrases.es: Esta noche deja el móvil abajo.
phrases.ph: EHS-tah NOH-cheh DEH-hah ehl MOH-beel ah-BAH-hoh
phrases.note: Abajo = 'downstairs' and arriba = 'upstairs'. Esta noche means 'tonight' — literally 'this night'.

phrases.en: Can you turn it up a bit?
phrases.note: Subir ('to go up') is how you turn up the volume. Subirlo = subir + lo ('it'). The opposite is bajarlo.
Compartir = 'to share'; with 'don't' it becomes no compartas. 'Online' is simply en internet.

phrases.en: Look at me, not your phone.
phrases.es: Mírame a mí, no al móvil.
phrases.ph: MEE-rah-meh ah mee, noh ahl MOH-beel
phrases.note: Mírame = mira ('look') + me. Adding a mí ('at me') gives extra emphasis — it's a bit firm.
In Spain a mobile phone is el móvil. In Latin America it's el celular, so móvil marks you as learning Spain Spanish.
Visto is the odd 'seen' form of ver (to see) — not vido. ¿Has visto...? is a great opener for anything you've lost.
Literally 'Can you call me on the mobile?' Spanish says call me (me llamar) rather than 'ring my phone'. Llamar starts with a 'y' sound.
Literally 'My phone has no battery'. Don't say muerto — Spanish phones don't 'die'. The stress in batería falls on the accented í.
Cargador comes from cargar, 'to charge' (or 'to load'). The -dor ending often means 'the thing that does it', like secador (hairdryer).
The h in has is silent, so it's just 'as'. Put anything after ¿Has visto mi...? — mi sudadera, mis llaves.
Spanish flips it: 'Will you lend me your charger?' Prestar means 'to lend'. ¿Me prestas...? is the go-to way to borrow anything.

phrases.ph: kwahl ehs lah kohn-trah-SEH-nyah dehl WEE-fee
phrases.note: Contraseña is 'password'. In Spain both i's in wifi sound like 'ee', not like English 'why'. Use ¿Cuál es...? (not ¿Qué es...?) when asking for a specific detail.
Funcionar is the word for machines 'working'. Don't use trabajar here — that's only for people working at a job.
Things 'go' slow in Spanish: va lento, literally 'goes slow'. Internet often has no 'el' in front, and the stress goes on the last syllable.

phrases.en: Can you turn off the time limit?
phrases.ph: PWEH-dehs kee-TAHR ehl LEE-mee-teh deh TYEHM-poh
phrases.note: Quitar means 'to remove' or 'take off'. Tiempo is 'time' as in an amount of time — for clock time you'd use hora.
Literally 'Will you give me more time?' ¿Me das...? is a really common, friendly way to ask for things — ¿Me das un vaso?
Más goes after the number: cinco minutos más, 'five minutes more'. In Spain, the c in cinco is a soft 'th'.
¿Por qué? (two words) means 'why?', while porque (one word) means 'because'. Lo is 'it' and comes before has.
El instituto (or el insti for short) is secondary school in Spain. El colegio is usually primary school.
Amigas means female friends. If any boys are in the group, it becomes amigos. Note Spanish says talking 'with' (con), not 'to'.
Casi means 'nearly'. Ya casi together is a very common 'almost there!' — you can also just say Ya casi on its own.

phrases.en: Wait, I'm just replying to someone.
phrases.note: Contestar is 'to reply'. The little a before alguien (someone) is needed whenever a person receives the action.
Quedar here means 'to have left': no me queda batería = 'I've got no battery left'. Works for anything — no me queda dinero.
Tu without an accent means 'your'; tú with an accent means 'you'. They sound the same, so it only matters when writing.
There's no verb for 'to hotspot', so Spanish says 'Can you share internet with me?' You'll also hear ¿Me compartes datos? (share data).
Quedarse sin means 'to run out of'. Datos is mobile data. Also handy: me he quedado sin batería.

phrases.es: Se me ha roto la pantalla.
phrases.ph: seh meh ah RROH-toh lah pahn-TAH-yah
phrases.note: Roto is 'broken', from romper. Se me ha... means it happened to you, by accident — handy for owning up gently.
Descargar is 'to download' — literally 'unload'. In chat, people shorten aplicación to la app.
Recibir means 'to receive'. Mensaje ends in -e but is masculine: el mensaje. A WhatsApp message is often just un whatsapp.
Mandar is the everyday word for 'to send' (enviar is more formal). El enlace is 'the link', though many just say el link.
Reiniciar is 'to restart' — re + iniciar (to start), just like English. Router is borrowed from English, said the Spanish way.
Lee means 'read!', but 'don't read' becomes no leas. 'Don't' commands swap the ending vowel, e to a for -er verbs like leer.

phrases.en: Can you top up my phone?
phrases.note: Recargar means 'to top up' credit — and also 'to recharge'. Say recargar el saldo if you want to be clear it's credit.

phrases.es: Deja de molestar a tu hermano.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh moh-lehs-TAHR ah too ehr-MAH-noh
phrases.note: Deja de + verb = 'stop ...ing' — deja de gritar (stop shouting). Molestar means 'to annoy', not 'molest' — a classic false friend.

phrases.es: Deja en paz a tu hermano.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah ehn pahth ah too ehr-MAH-noh
phrases.note: Literally 'leave your brother in peace'. The little a before tu hermano is needed whenever a person is on the receiving end.
Dejad (ending in -d) is for talking to two or more people — in Spain that's the 'you lot' form. To just one person it's deja de discutir.
Los dos = 'the two of you / both'. Parad is 'stop!' said to more than one person; to one person it's para.
Pasar means 'to happen' (as well as 'to pass'). In Spain, for something that's just happened, people say ha pasado ('has happened').
Hecho is the irregular 'done' form of hacer — not hacido. The h is silent, so it starts with the e sound.
Él (with an accent) means 'he'; el without one means 'the'. Putting él at the end stresses it: what did HE do?
Spanish 'throws the blame' on someone: echar la culpa. La culpa = 'the blame/fault' — no es mi culpa means 'it's not my fault'.
Devolver means 'to give back / return'. Here it's the command devuelve with lo ('it') glued on the end.
Suyo can mean 'his', 'hers' or 'theirs'. If it's unclear, say Eso es de él ('that's his') instead.
Same Spanish as 'That's his' — suyo covers both. To be clear it's a girl's, say Eso es de ella.
Antes de + verb = 'before ...ing'. Coger ('to take/grab') is everyday in Spain, but avoid it in Latin America, where it's rude.
Sé (with an accent) is the command 'be!'. Buena is for a girl — say sé bueno to a boy.
Picar means 'to sting' or 'bite', so it's 'stop stinging him'. You'll also hear deja de chincharle — same meaning, very Spain.
Literally 'don't pay him attention' — hacer caso means 'to take notice'. ¡Hazme caso! means 'Listen to me!'
Deja + lo ('it'). Déjalo works for a thing ('put it down') and for an argument ('drop it'). Said sharply, it can sound irritated.
A strong, firm 'that's enough!'. For extra force, parents in Spain say ¡Ya basta! ('Enough now!').

phrases.en: I don't care who started it.
phrases.note: Me da igual = 'I don't mind / I don't care' — literally 'it gives me the same'. Super useful: Me da igual, tú eliges (I don't mind, you choose).
Arreglar means 'to fix / sort out'. Arreglad is for two or more people, plus lo ('it'). To one person: arréglalo.
Literally 'ask for forgiveness' — pedir means 'to ask for'. The apology itself is Perdón or Lo siento.
Here déjale means 'leave him' (not 'let him'). Un poco de = 'a bit of' — un poco de agua, un poco de silencio.

phrases.en: Go away for five minutes and calm down.
phrases.note: Vete = 'go away' and cálmate = 'calm yourself down'. On its own, vete can sound harsh, so tone matters.
Gritar = 'to shout', and un grito is 'a shout' or 'a scream'. To two or more people: dejad de gritar.

phrases.en: Don't talk to him like that.
phrases.note: Así means 'like that / this way'. Le is 'to him' — for a girl it's still le: no le hables así works for both.
Por turnos = 'in turns'. Asking whose turn it is? ¿A quién le toca? — and 'it's my turn' is me toca a mí.
Compartid is 'share!' to two or more people, with lo ('it') on the end. To just one: compártelo.
Chivarse is Spain slang for 'to tell on someone', and a telltale is un chivato (or una chivata for a girl).

phrases.en: You're both as bad as each other.
phrases.note: Tal para cual is an idiom meaning 'two of a kind'. Sois is 'you are' when talking to two or more people.
Pide + se ('him') + lo ('it') = 'ask him for it'. Bien here means 'nicely / properly'. Also works for asking a girl.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, you two.
phrases.note: Literally 'you two, lower your voice'. Vosotros is 'you' for a group — use vosotras if both are girls.

phrases.en: That's not how we talk to each other.
phrases.note: Nos hablamos = 'we talk to each other'. The nos does the job of 'each other' — nos queremos means 'we love each other'.
Putting él (he) at the end points the finger: 'HE started it'. Empezar = to start.
No need for él here — está already means 'he is'. Add él only to stress who.
Dile = 'tell him' (di + le). Dile que + verb is a handy pattern: dile que se vaya = tell him to go away.
Sal = 'get out', from salir. It's short and sharp — exactly how it's shouted.
Copiar = to copy. The me sticks onto the end: copiarme = copy me.
Mío = mine. It changes for feminine things: la sudadera es mía.
Justo = fair. Looks like 'just', as in justice. The ultimate sibling complaint.

phrases.es: Él siempre se sale con la suya.
phrases.ph: ehl SYEHM-preh seh SAH-leh kohn lah SOO-yah
phrases.note: Salirse con la suya = to get your own way. A set phrase — just learn it as a chunk.
Pesado literally means 'heavy' but is Spain's go-to word for an annoying person. For a girl: pesada.
Said straight to him. Qué + adjective = 'so…!': qué pesado, qué tonto. Cheeky, not nasty.
Literally 'leave me in peace'. Déjame = leave me (deja + me).
Swap mamá for papá if Dad's around. Molestar = to annoy or bother — not the English 'molest'.
Pegar = to hit. It also means 'to stick', like pegamento (glue) — context makes it clear.
Estaba = 'I was' (somewhere). Primero = first. Great for sofa wars.
One word packed together: devuelve (give back) + me + lo (it). Use devuélvemela for a feminine thing.
Para = 'stop' (from parar). Ya adds urgency — like 'stop it NOW'.
Vete = 'go away', from irse. Short and a bit harsh; ¡Vete de aquí! = get out of here!
Mirar = to look at — no extra word for 'at'. Estar + -ando = '-ing': está mirando = is looking.
Cosas = things, the everyday word for 'stuff'. No toques = don't touch, said to one person.
Mentir = to lie (not tell the truth). Una mentira = a lie; mentiroso = liar.
Cállate = 'shut up', from callarse. It's rude — fine with a brother, not with a parent or teacher.
Tocar here means 'to be someone's turn'. Me toca = my turn; te toca = your turn.
Coger = to take or grab — totally normal in Spain. Cargador = phone charger.
Crío = little kid, a teasing word in Spain. For a girl it's cría. Mildly mean — sibling level.
In Spain people often say le for 'him' here (in other places, lo). Yo at the start = 'I didn't!'.
¿Dónde está...? = 'Where is...?' — for people, pets or things. Always está (not es) when asking where something is.
Roll the rr in perro! A single r gives pero, which means 'but'. A female dog is la perra.
Visto is the irregular 'seen' form of ver. The a before Monty is there because he's a person — well, a much-loved pet.
Dejar + verb = 'to let (someone) do something'. So dejar salir = 'let out' and dejar entrar = 'let in'.
Al is a + el squashed together. Spanish always does this: a el perro becomes al perro.
Salir means 'to go out' — you'll see salida (exit) on signs. Just swap entrar for salir to flip 'let in' to 'let out'.

phrases.en: Can you take Monty for a walk?
phrases.ph: PWEH-dehs sah-KAHR ah pah-seh-AHR ah MOHN-tee
phrases.note: Sacar a pasear = 'take out for a walk'. Many people just say ¿Puedes sacar a Monty? — sacar al perro means walking the dog.

phrases.en: Has Monty been for a walk?
phrases.note: Literally 'has Monty gone out to walk?'. Pasear is a gentle stroll; a walk is un paseo.
Literally 'have they given him to eat?'. Spanish often uses 'they' like this where English says 'has he been...'.

phrases.ph: PWEH-dehs dahr deh koh-MEHR ahl PEH-rroh
phrases.note: Spanish has no single verb for 'feed' in everyday speech — you 'give to eat': dar de comer. Dar de beber = 'give a drink'.
Dale = da ('give') + le ('him'). No word for 'some' needed — Spanish just says 'give him water'.

phrases.es: Su cuenco de agua está vacío.
phrases.ph: soo KWEHN-koh deh AH-gwah ehs-TAH bah-THEE-oh
phrases.note: Un cuenco is a bowl, and cuenco de agua is literally 'bowl of water'. Vacío = 'empty'; the opposite is lleno (full).
La correa is a dog lead — it also means a strap or belt. Su can mean 'his', 'her' or 'their'.
Ponle = pon ('put') + le ('on him'). Spanish says 'put him the lead' instead of 'his lead'. Take it off: quítale la correa.
'Let him' is deja salir, but with 'don't' it changes to no dejes. The le ('him') moves in front of dejes.
La verja is a metal garden gate (a wooden one is often la cancela or la puerta del jardín). La puerta on its own means a door.
Llamar means 'to call' — shouting for someone or phoning them. It's also in me llamo ('I'm called').
Bajar = 'to get down', so this is 'get him down from the sofa'. Del is de + el joined up. Stress the end of sofá, as the accent shows.
Just 'What does he have?'. Add en la boca if Monty's chewing something: ¿Qué tiene en la boca? (What's he got in his mouth?).
Quitar means 'to take away / remove'; the le means 'from him'. Quítate la chaqueta = 'take your jacket off'.
Deja de + verb = 'stop ...ing'. La comida means 'food', but also 'lunch' — the main midday meal in Spain.
Literally 'don't give him that'. 'Give him' is dale, but with 'don't' it becomes no le des.
Hacer pis = 'to do a wee' — a casual, family-friendly phrase. Tiene que = 'he has to / needs to'.
La caca is the everyday (not rude) word for poo. Recoger = 'to pick up', same as recoge tu ropa.
Llévate = 'take with you'. Llevar is for taking something along; traer is for bringing something here.
Ladrar = 'to bark'. No word for 'he' is needed — ladra already means 'he barks'. A dog's woof is guau guau.

phrases.es: Tiene las patas llenas de barro.
phrases.ph: TYEH-neh lahs PAH-tahs YEH-nahs deh BAH-rroh
phrases.note: Literally 'he has his paws full of mud'. Animals have patas (paws/legs); people have piernas (legs) and pies (feet).
Seca ('dry') + le ('his / for him'). Spanish says 'dry him the paws' rather than 'his paws'. Sécate = 'dry yourself'.

phrases.en: Don't let him on the bed.
phrases.es: No le dejes subir a la cama.
phrases.ph: noh leh DEH-hehs soo-BEER ah lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Literally 'don't let him climb up onto the bed'. Subir a = 'to get up on', like subir al sofá.
Literally 'have you given him the tablet?'. La pastilla is a pill or tablet — not una tableta, which is the gadget.
Siéntate means 'sit down' — for dogs and people. Other commands: ¡quieto! (stay!), ¡ven! (come!).
Un premio normally means 'a prize', but it's also the usual word for a dog treat — a little reward.
Vomitar = 'to be sick' (throw up). Estar malo means ill in general, so use ha vomitado for the messy kind.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.ph: MOHN-tee PWEH-deh dohr-MEER ehn mee KWAHR-toh
phrases.note: Cuarto = 'bedroom' in everyday Spain Spanish. Habitación works too and sounds a bit more formal.
The me in me ha robado means 'from me'. Swap the thing: me ha robado el boli = he stole my pen.

phrases.en: Do I have to walk him?
phrases.note: Sacar a pasear = 'take out for a walk'. Just sacar al perro is also what people say in Spain.
Mono = 'cute' in Spain (it also means monkey!). For a girl or female dog it's mona.
Apestar = 'to stink'. Also try huele fatal = 'he smells awful'.
Un baño is a bath, but el baño also means the bathroom. Bañar al perro = to bath the dog.
Buen chico = 'good boy'. Buen drops the o when it comes before the noun: un chico bueno, but un buen chico.

phrases.ph: AHL-gyehn leh ah DAH-doh deh koh-MEHR
phrases.note: Dar de comer = 'to feed' (literally 'give to eat'). Le = 'him' here.
Ladrar = 'to bark'. Otra vez = 'again' — handy for moaning about anything.
Bájate = 'get down'. Bajar is 'to go down'; the te on the end makes it an order to him.
Dog owners in Spain often shorten siéntate to just ¡sienta! when training.
Ven = 'come' (an order to one person or dog). Aquí = 'here'. Works on your brother too.
Soltar = 'to let go'. ¡Suelta! is the classic dog command; to a person you'd say ¡suéltalo!
Bonito = 'lovely' — Spanish owners praise dogs with muy bien plus a pet name. Bonita for a female dog.
Chupar = 'to lick' or 'to suck'. Lamer is the dictionary word, but chupar is what you'll hear.

phrases.es: Otra vez está en mi cama.
phrases.ph: OH-trah behth ehs-TAH ehn mee KAH-mah
phrases.note: Putting otra vez first makes it sound more fed up. Mi cama = 'my bed'.

phrases.en: Can I give him a treat?
phrases.note: Un premio = 'a prize', but it's also the word for a dog treat. Le = 'to him'.

phrases.en: It's not my turn to walk him.
phrases.note: Me toca = 'it's my turn'. No me toca = 'not my turn' — the perfect excuse for any chore.
Déjalo = 'leave it'. The lo means 'it', whatever he's got in his mouth.
Adónde is 'where to' — it's a + dónde stuck together, used when someone is moving somewhere. Vas comes from ir (to go).
Spanish puts 'with' first: con quién = 'with whom'. You can't leave con dangling at the end like in English.
Va means 'goes' (he/she goes). If you expect several people, you can ask ¿Quiénes van? — the plural 'who'.

phrases.en: What are you going to do?
phrases.note: Vas a + an action = 'you're going to...' — a really easy way to talk about plans: vas a comer, vas a salir. The h in hacer is silent.
¿A qué hora...? means 'at what time...?' — stick any verb after it: ¿A qué hora sales? ¿A qué hora empieza?

phrases.en: What time will you be back?
phrases.note: Vuelves is from volver (to come back). Spanish often uses the present tense for future plans, so 'what time do you come back?' works fine.
Literally 'how are you going to go?'. Answers are easy: en autobús, en coche, andando (on foot).
There's no single word for 'a lift' here — you say 'do you need me to take you?'. Lleve is from llevar (to take someone somewhere).

phrases.en: Do you want me to take you?
phrases.note: ¿Quieres que...? = 'Do you want me to...?' — a handy offer pattern: ¿Quieres que te ayude? (want me to help you?).
Recoger means 'to pick up' — people and things. Literally this is 'do I have to pick you up?'; the te on the end means 'you'.

phrases.en: Message me when you get there.
phrases.note: Escríbeme is 'write to me' — the usual way to say 'text/message me'. After cuando for the future, llegas changes to llegues.

phrases.en: Let me know if your plans change.
phrases.note: Avísame means 'let me know' or 'give me a heads-up' — from avisar (to warn/tell). Really useful on its own too.
Encendido means 'switched on' (from encender). The opposite is apagado — 'off'. In Spain a mobile is always el móvil.

phrases.en: Make sure your phone has some charge.
phrases.es: Asegúrate de que el móvil tenga batería.
phrases.ph: ah-seh-GOO-rah-teh deh keh ehl MOH-beel TEHN-gah bah-teh-REE-ah
phrases.note: Asegúrate de que = 'make sure that'. Spanish talks about 'battery' (batería) rather than 'charge'.
Suficiente = 'enough', and it goes before the noun. In Spain the ci is said with a 'th' sound, like in 'think'.
Spanish says 'the coat' (el abrigo), not 'your coat', when it's obvious whose it is. Same with el móvil, las llaves.
Lleva is from llevar — 'to take with you' or 'to wear'. Don't use tomar here; that's for taking food, drink or a bus.
Weather uses hace ('it makes'): hace frío (cold), hace calor (hot), hace sol (sunny). Don't say está frío for the weather.
Lloviendo comes from llover (to rain). Está + an -ando/-iendo word = 'is ...ing', happening right now.
Literally 'don't arrive very late'. Llegar (to arrive) becomes llegues after no when telling someone not to do something.
Word for word it's 'have care' — ten comes from tener (to have). Say it as someone heads out the door.
Literally 'pass it well' — pasarlo bien means 'to have a good time'. To a group, say pasadlo bien.
Hasta = 'until', luego = 'later'. People in Spain use it all the time, even as a simple 'bye' to a shop assistant.
Quedar is the Spain word for 'to arrange to meet'. Habéis is the 'you lot' form, since she's meeting friends.
In Spain 'to drive' is conducir. You'll hear manejar in Latin America, but not here.

phrases.en: Will there be an adult there?
phrases.note: Va a haber = 'there's going to be' — the future of hay (there is). Algún means 'any' or 'some'.
