Quedaos is 'you lot, stay'. Juntas is for a group of girls — use juntos if any boys are in the group.

phrases.en: Don't go off on your own.
phrases.note: Sola means 'alone' for a girl — say solo to a boy. Vayas is the 'don't' form of irse (to go off).
Llévate = 'take with you'. The -te on the end makes it personal, like 'take them along'. In Spain ll sounds like the y in 'yes'.
Llamar means 'to call' (phone someone). It's the same verb as in me llamo — literally 'I call myself'.
A casa = 'home' when you're going there, no 'the' needed. -mente works like '-ly': directamente = 'directly'.

phrases.en: I'll pick you up at ten.
phrases.note: Recojo is 'I pick up' — the g in recoger turns into j to keep the soft sound. Times use a las: a las diez = 'at ten'.

phrases.en: Say hi to them from me.
phrases.note: Recuerdos literally means 'memories', but dar recuerdos is the Spanish way to send your best wishes to someone.
Handy pattern: ¿Puedo + verb? = 'Can I...?' Salir means 'to go out' or 'to leave', so this is all you need to ask.
Podemos is 'we can' (from poder). Swap puedo (I can) for podemos when you're asking for you and your friends.
Llevar means 'to take' someone somewhere. The me goes at the front: me puedes llevar = 'you can take me?'

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift?
phrases.note: Spanish has no special word for 'a lift' here — you just ask 'can you take me?' Add a + place, e.g. ¿Me puedes llevar al centro?
Recoger means 'to pick up' — both a person from somewhere and things off the floor. The g here is a throaty sound, like the ch in Scottish 'loch'.
Just swap me (me) for nos (us). Spanish usually leaves out 'there' when it's obvious — add allí if you want to point it out.

phrases.en: Can you pick us up later?
phrases.note: Luego is the everyday word for 'later' in Spain. You'll also hear it in hasta luego, 'see you later'.
Amiga is a girl friend — say mi amigo for a boy. Notice Spanish puts the person at the end: 'can come my friend?'

phrases.en: Can I have a friend over?
phrases.ph: PWEH-deh beh-NEER OO-nah ah-MEE-gah ah KAH-sah
phrases.note: Spanish doesn't say 'have someone over' — it asks 'can a friend come home?' A casa means 'home' (to the house). Use un amigo for a boy.
No word for 'she' is needed — puede already means 'can she/he'. Venir is 'to come' towards where you are.
Quedarse means 'to stay'. Cenar is a verb, 'to have dinner', so a cenar is literally 'to dine' — no word for 'dinner' needed.

phrases.es: ¿Se puede quedar a dormir esta noche?
phrases.ph: seh PWEH-deh keh-DAHR ah dohr-MEER EHS-tah NOH-cheh
phrases.note: Quedarse a dormir = 'stay to sleep', which is how Spanish says 'stay over'. Esta noche is 'tonight' (literally 'this night').

phrases.en: Can I stay at her house?
phrases.ph: meh PWEH-doh keh-DAHR ehn soo KAH-sah
phrases.note: Su can mean 'her', 'his' or 'their', so en su casa works for any friend. Me puedo quedar = 'can I stay'.
There's no single word for 'sleepover' in everyday Spanish — quedarse a dormir ('stay to sleep') does the job.

phrases.en: What time do I have to be home?
phrases.es: ¿A qué hora tengo que estar en casa?
phrases.ph: ah keh OH-rah TEHN-goh keh ehs-TAHR ehn KAH-sah
phrases.note: Tengo que + verb = 'I have to...'. Don't forget the a at the start: ¿A qué hora...? means 'At what time...?'

phrases.en: Do I have to come home that early?
phrases.note: Volver means 'to come back'. Pronto here means 'early', and tan pronto is 'so early' — a classic teen complaint.

phrases.es: Todos los demás se quedan hasta más tarde.
phrases.ph: TOH-dohs lohs deh-MAHS seh KEH-dahn AHS-tah mahs TAHR-deh
phrases.note: Los demás means 'the others' or 'everyone else'. Hasta más tarde = 'until later' — the h in hasta is silent.
Literally 'I write to you'. Spanish often uses the present tense for things you'll do soon, so no 'will' word is needed.
Avisar means 'to let someone know' or 'warn'. Te aviso is short and very common — parents say avísame, 'let me know'.
Camino means 'way' or 'path', so de camino is 'on the way'. Perfect for a quick text home.
Salimos is 'we leave' (from salir). Ya after it means 'right now' — it's snappier than ahora.
Literally 'already almost we have arrived'. Casi means 'almost' and llegar is 'to arrive'.
Adding ya gives the sense 'I've arrived' rather than just 'I'm here'. Aquí is 'here' — put the stress on the last part.
Fuera means 'outside' or 'out'. Use estoy (not soy) for where you are — estar is the 'where' verb.
Dónde = 'where', estás = 'you are'. The accent means you stress the end of estás; without it, estas means 'these'.
Tardar means 'to take (time)'. Vas a tardar = 'you're going to take', so this asks 'how much are you going to take?'
Darse prisa = 'to hurry' (literally 'give yourself hurry'). The quick parent version is ¡Date prisa!

phrases.en: Can I go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Cine is 'cinema' — in Spain the c sounds like 'th'. Swap in al parque (park) or a la bolera (bowling).

phrases.en: I'm going to my friend's house.
phrases.es: Voy a casa de mi amiga.
phrases.ph: boy ah KAH-sah deh mee ah-MEE-gah
phrases.note: Spanish says 'the house of my friend' — no apostrophe-s. Amiga is a girl; use mi amigo for a boy.
Quedar is the Spain word for arranging to meet friends: hemos quedado = 'we've arranged to meet'. ¿Quedamos? = 'Shall we meet up?'

phrases.en: Can I go to a party on Saturday?
phrases.es: ¿Puedo ir a una fiesta el sábado?
phrases.ph: PWEH-doh eer ah OO-nah FYEHS-tah ehl SAH-bah-doh
phrases.note: El sábado means 'on Saturday' — Spanish uses el instead of 'on' for days. Fiesta is any party.
Cumpleaños comes from cumplir años, 'to complete years'. It always ends in -s, even for one birthday.

phrases.es: Esta noche me quedo en casa.
phrases.ph: EHS-tah NOH-cheh meh KEH-doh ehn KAH-sah
phrases.note: Me quedo en casa = 'I'm staying at home'. Spanish has no 'stay in' — you say where you're staying.

phrases.en: Her mum will bring me back.
phrases.es: Su madre me trae de vuelta.
phrases.ph: soo MAH-dreh meh TRAH-eh deh BWEHL-tah
phrases.note: De vuelta means 'back' (on the return trip). Trae is 'brings' — present tense, but it means 'will bring'.

phrases.en: Can I stay a bit longer?
phrases.note: Un poco más = 'a little more'. It works for loads of things: ¿Puedo jugar un poco más? (play a bit longer).
Antes de las diez = 'before ten'. Times use las because it's las horas: a las diez = 'at ten'.

phrases.en: Wait for me in the car.
phrases.note: Espera + me joined together = 'wait for me'. Coche is the Spain word for 'car' (Latin America says carro or auto).
Ven is the short command from venir (to come). It's irregular, so it doesn't look like viene — just learn ven.
Vete comes from irse (to leave/go off). It's blunt — like 'go away!' — so it can sound rude if you're not joking.
From esperar, which means both 'to wait' and 'to hope'. Add un momento to make it softer: Espera un momento.
Ahí means 'there' (near you). Don't mix it up with hay (there is) — ahí has two separate vowel sounds, with the stress on the í.
Escucha comes from escuchar (to listen). Oye ('hey, listen') is a more casual way to grab someone's attention.
Mira is from mirar (to look). Spanish speakers also say it at the start of a sentence, like 'look, ...' before explaining something.
Para here is from parar (to stop) — not the word para meaning 'for'. Say it short and sharp, stressing the first syllable.
Spanish has no one-word 'don't' — a firm no does the job. Say it sharply and it works just like a warning.
Hagas is from hacer (to do). With no in front, the command changes form: haz (do) becomes no hagas (don't do).
Deja (leave) + lo (it) joined into one word. It also means 'forget it' or 'drop it' in an argument.
Literally 'leave it there'. Spanish uses dejar (to leave) for putting something down, rather than a separate 'put down' verb.
Three words in one: da (give) + me (to me) + lo (it). The accent keeps the stress on the first syllable even though the word got longer.
Trae (bring) + lo (it). Traer is 'bring towards me'; llevar is 'take away from here' — easy to mix up.
Toma on its own is what you say while handing something over — like 'here you go'. No need for 'this'.
Sujeta is from sujetar (to hold firmly). Don't confuse esto (this thing) with está (is) — esto is stressed at the start, está at the end.
Ayuda (help) + me. Add por favor and it's a polite request; on its own it can sound like a cry for help.
Cuidado means 'care' — shouted on its own it's the quick warning, like 'watch out!' or 'careful!'.
Ten cuidado con... = 'be careful with...': ten cuidado con el cuchillo (the knife). Calmer than just ¡Cuidado!
Literally 'give yourself hurry' — prisa means 'rush'. Tengo prisa means 'I'm in a hurry'.
Just 'more slowly'. Handy when someone's speaking Spanish too fast too: Más despacio, por favor.
Calma + te ('calm yourself'). Like in English, telling someone to calm down can wind them up more — tranquila is gentler.
Literally 'in serious?'. Works for surprise or disbelief, exactly like 'seriously?' — the tone does the work.
Haces literally means 'do you do', but Spanish uses it for 'what are you doing (right now)?' too. The h is silent.
Has hecho = 'you have done'. Hecho is the odd 'done' form of hacer — and both h's are silent, so has sounds just like 'as'.
Two words with an accent means 'why?'. Written as one word, porque, it means 'because' — a classic GCSE mix-up.
¿Cómo? also means 'pardon?' when you didn't hear someone — much politer than ¿Qué?
Dónde = 'where (is it)'; adónde = 'where to'. So ¿Dónde está? but ¿Adónde vas?
Question words carry an accent: cuándo (when?). Without it, cuando just means 'when' in a sentence — cuando llegues.
Dicho is the 'said' form of decir. In Spain, ha dicho ('has said') is normal for something that just happened.
Literally 'what do you want to say?' — querer decir is how Spanish says 'to mean'. ¿Qué quiere decir...? = 'What does ... mean?'
Ya = 'already'. Word order is 'already to-you it I-have said' — te and lo go before he dicho.

phrases.es: Te lo he pedido tres veces.
phrases.ph: teh loh eh peh-DEE-doh trehs BEH-thehs
phrases.note: Pedir means 'to ask for' something (a favour); preguntar is 'to ask' a question. Veces is the plural of vez (time).
Spanish flips the order: 'now not'. Same trick with Hoy no (not today) and Aquí no (not here).
Word for word the same as English. People also say ahora voy ('coming now') when they mean 'in a minute'.
Luego = 'later' or 'afterwards'. Más tarde also means 'later' and is a bit more definite.
Literally 'it can be'. Quizás is the one-word 'maybe' you'll see in textbooks — both are fine.
Veremos = 'we will see' (from ver). The ya adds a 'let's wait and see' feel — as with parents everywhere, it often means no.
Literally 'in no way'. Very firm. For a casual version, Spanish speakers say ni hablar ('don't even talk about it').
Vale is Spain's everyday 'OK'. Say it with a flat, fed-up tone and it's the sulky 'fine'. The v sounds like a soft b.
Venga literally means 'come', but in Spain it's used for 'go on', 'come on' or 'alright then'. Hear it everywhere.
Sounds like 'it's fine now', but said firmly it means 'that's enough, stop it'. A very common parent line in Spain.
Mira (look) + me. No separate word for 'at' — mirar already means 'to look at'.
Cállate is closer to 'shut up' — it can sound rude. Silencio, por favor or Baja la voz is gentler.
Literally 'lower the voice'. Bajar (to lower) is also used for music and the TV: baja la música.
Contesta (answer) + me. The accent appears because the word got longer, but the stress stays in the same place.

phrases.en: Don't talk to me like that.
phrases.note: Así means 'like that' or 'this way' — really useful: hazlo así (do it like this). Hablas becomes hables after no.
Una broma is 'a joke' or 'a prank'. Estar de broma = 'to be joking'; ¿Estás de broma? = 'Are you kidding?'
Claro means 'clear', but on its own it's the everyday 'of course' or 'sure'. Claro que sí = 'of course, yes'.
¿Qué? = 'what?'. Fine at home, but can sound blunt — ¿qué pasa? ('what's up?') is softer.
Voy literally means 'I'm going', but Spanish uses it where English says 'Coming!'. Yell ¡Ya voy! if they keep calling.
Espera = 'wait'. Shorter and more casual: ¡un momento! or just ¡espera!
Adding que in front makes it 'I said NO!' — great when someone won't listen. Works with sí too: ¡que sí!
Por qué = 'why' (two words, with an accent). Porque written as one word means 'because'.
Ahora voy = 'I'm coming now' — but in Spain it often means 'in a bit'. Parents know this trick.
Vale = 'okay', the most Spain word there is. Uf is the Spanish 'ugh'. Say it slowly for maximum sulk.
Déjalo ya = 'stop it now'. Ya adds 'already/now' and makes it sound impatient.
Quítate = 'get out of the way'. A bit rude — fine for your brother, less so for a teacher.
Devolver = 'to give back'. Me = 'to me', lo = 'it', all glued on the end: devuélve-me-lo.
Spanish speakers say ¡chis! or ¡chsss! to shush someone. Add ¡callaos! to tell a group to be quiet.
Ocupada = 'busy' — ocupada is for a girl, a boy says ocupado.
Date prisa = 'give yourself hurry'. In Spain you'll also hear ¡venga, va! to rush someone.
Mira = 'look'. Spanish speakers also start sentences with mira just to get attention, like 'listen…'.
Lárgate = 'get lost' — stronger than vete. Fine with your brother, rude with anyone else.
Paso = 'I'll pass / can't be bothered'. Very Spain teen. Paso de ti = 'I'm ignoring you'.
Yo no = 'not me'. Flip it for yo sí = 'I did / me yes'. Handy when someone asks who broke something.
He sido = 'I have been'. Yo no he sido is the classic 'it wasn't me' line in Spain.
Espérame = 'wait for me'. The me stuck on the end means 'for me' — no extra word needed.
En paz = 'in peace'. Déjame en paz sounds dramatic — perfect for slamming a door.
Qué tal = 'how'. Even shorter: just ¿qué tal? works as a hello too.
¿Qué pasa? = 'what's happening?'. Can be a friendly hello or 'what's wrong?' depending on your tone.
¿Sabes qué? = 'do you know what?'. It's how you grab someone before news.
Ha ido = 'it went'. Swap in a thing: ¿qué tal el examen? = how was the exam?
Contar = 'to tell' (and 'to count'). Cuéntame = 'tell me' — an invite to spill everything.
¿Ah, sí? = 'oh really?' — lighter than ¿en serio?, just showing you're listening.
Qué + a describing word = 'how…!'. Qué bien, qué guay, qué pena — one pattern, loads of uses.
Ay is the Spanish 'oh' when something hurts or goes wrong. You'll hear ¡ay! all the time.
¿Qué te pasa? = 'what's happening to you?'. The te makes it personal — 'what's up with you?'.
Era = 'was' for describing something ongoing. Use it after a call or a knock at the door.
Opinar = 'to think / have an opinion'. Putting tú first stresses 'you', as in 'what do YOU think?'.
Literally 'I can't believe it to myself'. The me and lo are just how Spanish says it — learn it as one chunk.
Me voy = 'I'm off'. Add a + verb for why: me voy a dormir = I'm off to bed.
Spanish often uses the present for the near future: vuelvo = 'I'll be back'. Times use a las: a las seis.
Te quiero is what family says. Te amo is for big romantic moments — too much for your mum.
Andar = 'to walk', but andar haciendo means 'to be up to'. Sounds relaxed and chatty.
¿Qué tal + thing? is the quickest way to ask how something went: ¿qué tal el insti?
Estar is used for how you feel right now. Estoy bien = I'm fine.
Cansado = 'tired' — that's for a dad. A mum says cansada.
Vaya + noun = 'what a…!'. ¡Vaya lío! = what a mess. Very common in Spain.
Ya here means 'now/already' — it adds the sense of 'I'm back'. En casa = 'at home'.
Preocuparse = 'to worry'. No te preocupes is the go-to comfort line. For a group: no os preocupéis.
¿Va todo bien? = 'is everything going well?'. Ir (to go) is used for how things are going.
Orgulloso = 'proud' — dad form. A mum says orgullosa. De ti = 'of you'.

phrases.en: Did you have a good time?
phrases.note: Pasarlo bien = 'to have a good time'. Pásalo bien = 'have fun'.
Papá has the stress on the last syllable — that's what the accent on the á shows. Stress the first syllable instead and you're saying 'potato' in Latin America!
Mamá is stressed on the end, shown by the accent. Spanish questions also get an upside-down ¿ at the start when you write them.
¿Qué? on its own can sound a bit sharp. If you just didn't hear, ¿Cómo? or ¿Qué has dicho? ('What did you say?') is softer.
Haces comes from hacer ('to do/make'). Spanish often uses the simple 'you do' form where English says 'are you doing'.
Spanish has two verbs for 'to be'. For where someone or something is, always use estar — so estás, never eres.
Adónde means 'where to' — use it with vas (you go, from ir). Just dónde means 'where' for something staying put.
Está means 'is' for a location. Mind the accent: está (is) and esta (this) sound different — the stress moves to the end.
Handy pattern: ¿Dónde está + name/thing? works for anything — ¿Dónde está el mando? ('Where's the remote?').
Names don't change in Spanish. You could also ask ¿Dónde está el perro? ('Where's the dog?').
Hora means 'hour' or 'time', and the h is silent. The answer starts Es la una... or Son las dos...
Día ends in -a but it's a boy word: el día. That's why you say buenos días, not buenas.
Salimos is 'we leave' from salir. The a at the start means 'at' — ¿A qué hora...? = 'At what time...?' for any plan.
Hoy means 'today' — the h is silent, so it sounds just like English 'oi'. Hacemos is 'we do' from hacer.
Algún sitio means 'somewhere/anywhere'. Sitio ('place') is the everyday word in Spain; lugar means the same but is a bit more formal.
Ya at the end adds impatience, like 'now, already'. ¿Podemos + verb? = 'Can we...?' — a pattern you can reuse all the time.
Listo is for Dad — ask Mum ¿Estás lista? Careful: ser listo means 'to be clever', but estar listo means 'ready'.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: Tardar means 'to take (time)' — there's no single English word for it. ¿Cuánto vas a tardar? is literally 'How much are you going to take?'
Ven is the short 'you do it' form of venir (to come). Spanish says ven a ver — 'come to see' — instead of 'come and look'.
Mira comes from mirar (to look). No word for 'at' is needed — mira esto is simply 'look this'.
Spanish uses mirar for both 'look' and 'watch', so it's the same as 'Look at this'. Add ¡Mira, mira! to sound excited.
Escucha is from escuchar (to listen). Like mira, it needs no 'to' after it — escucha esto, 'listen this'.
Adivina is 'guess!' from adivinar — linked to adivino, a fortune-teller. ¿A que no sabes qué? is another fun way to say it.
Pasar means 'to happen' as well as 'to pass'. In Spain, ha pasado ('has happened') is used for things from today.
Adivinarás is 'you will guess' — the -ás ending shows the future. Nunca ('never') goes first, before the verb.
Qué + describing word = 'How...!' or 'That's so...!'. Gracioso means funny-haha; for funny-strange, say qué raro.
Raro means 'weird' or 'odd'. The r at the start of a word is rolled strongly in Spanish, so give it a good trill.
Fastidio means 'annoyance' or 'nuisance' — use it about a situation, like a flat battery. For an annoying person, say qué pesado/pesada.
Asco means 'disgust'. Teens in Spain say ¡qué asco! constantly — about food, bugs, or anything gross.
Vergüenza means 'shame/embarrassment'. The two dots on ü tell you to pronounce the u. Watch out — embarazada means pregnant!
Justo means 'fair'. The Spanish j is a throaty sound, like the ch in Scottish 'loch' — not the English j in 'just'.
Literally 'it gives me the same'. Me da igual is fairly neutral; no me importa can sound colder, so this is the safer choice.
Sé with an accent means 'I know' (from saber). Without the accent, se is a different little word — the accent matters in writing.
Literally 'it can be'. Quizás also means 'maybe', but puede ser works best as a one-word-style answer.
Watch out: seguramente looks like 'surely' but usually means 'probably'. The -mente ending is like English -ly.
Vale is very Spain-specific — you'll hear it in every conversation. Said flatly, it can sound like a sulky 'fine'.
In vale, the v sounds like a soft b — Spanish doesn't have a separate v sound. Say vale, vale to mean 'OK, OK, I get it'.
Literally 'what it may be'. Like 'whatever' in English, it sounds dismissive if you roll your eyes while saying it.
En serio is literally 'in serious'. It works as a question (¿En serio?) or to insist: Te lo digo en serio — 'I mean it'.
Verdad means 'truth', so this is 'of truth?'. The final d is very soft — almost like the th in 'the'.
¡Qué va! means 'no way, not at all' when disagreeing — '¿Estás cansada?' '¡Qué va!'. For amazed 'no way!', say ¡No me digas!
Obviamente is easy to spot — -mente = -ly. Claro ('of course') is shorter and even more common in chat.
Exacto is the quick way to agree. The x sounds like 'ks', as in English.
Ya lo sé is 'I already know it'. Said sharply it's the classic 'I know, stop telling me!' — so it can sound grumpy.
Para here is 'stop!' from parar — not the word para meaning 'for'. Say ¡Para ya! for 'Stop it now!'
Literally 'leave me in peace'. Deja + me join into one word, déjame. It's blunt, so expect a reaction if you say it to Mum or Dad!
Vete comes from irse (to go away) — the -te means 'yourself'. Short and rude-sounding; déjame un rato ('leave me a while') is gentler.
Pesada literally means 'heavy'. It's for Mum — say eres pesado to Dad or your brother.
Muy means 'very'. Use pesada for a female, pesado for a male. Qué pesada eres is an even more exasperated version.
In Spain the c in gracias is said like the th in 'think'. Swap in papá for Dad. Muchas gracias = 'thanks a lot'.
No quería is literally 'I didn't want to' — Spanish uses it for 'I didn't mean to'. Lo siento is a more heartfelt 'I'm sorry'.
Te quiero comes from querer ('to want/love'). It's what families say; te amo is for romantic love.
Aburrida is for a girl — a boy says aburrido. Careful: soy aburrida would mean 'I'm boring'!
Guay is the everyday Spain word for 'cool' — rhymes with 'why'. It never changes for boy/girl or plural.
Literally 'nothing happens'. Spaniards say no pasa nada all the time to mean 'no problem, it's OK'.
Preguntar means 'to ask a question' (pedir is to ask for something). Una cosa, 'a thing', is how Spanish says 'something' here.
Literally 'it's a joke'. Add que for 'I'm only joking!': ¡Que es broma!
Ya here means 'now' — 'I'm now home'. Many Spanish families shout just ¡Ya estoy aquí! ('I'm here!') as they come in.
Use yo también to agree with something positive. To agree with a negative ('Me neither'), say yo tampoco.
Estás comes from estar, the 'to be' used for how you feel right now. The easy answer is 'Sí, estoy bien' (Yes, I'm fine).
Literally 'what's happening to you?'. Pasar means 'to happen', and it's the everyday way to ask what's up.
Careful: disgustada means 'upset', not 'disgusted'. Te veo is 'I see you', so it's like 'you seem upset to me'. Say disgustado to a boy.
Encontrarse normally means 'to find yourself', but with bien or mal it's how Spanish people say they feel well or unwell.
Tirita is the word for a plaster in Spain (it means 'little strip'). In Latin America you'd hear curita instead.
Duele comes from doler (to hurt). Spanish says 'where does it hurt to you?', so the te is needed. '¿Te duele?' on its own means 'Does it hurt?'

phrases.en: Do you want to talk about it?
phrases.note: Ello means 'it' when you're talking about a situation, not a thing. The h in hablar is silent.
From preocuparse (to worry). Say every vowel in preocupes separately — Spanish doesn't blend them. Really handy for calming someone down.

phrases.en: Try not to stress about your exams.
phrases.es: Intenta no agobiarte con los exámenes.
phrases.ph: een-TEHN-tah noh ah-goh-BYAHR-teh kohn lohs ehk-SAH-meh-nehs
phrases.note: Agobiarse is the Spain word for getting stressed or overwhelmed. Intenta no + verb = 'try not to...'.
Deberías means 'you should' — a softer way to give advice than a straight order. Add any verb after it: deberías dormir, deberías comer.
Tener cara de... = 'to look...' (literally 'to have a face of'). Cansada is for a girl; for a boy it's cansado.
Encontrarse = 'to feel' when talking about health. Mejor = better, peor = worse.
Gruñona = 'grumpy' (a boy is gruñón). It comes from gruñir, to growl. Qué + word + estás is a handy way to tease.
Anímate = 'cheer up' or 'go on, get into it'. Same word to push someone to join in: ¡Anímate, ven con nosotros!
No seas... = 'don't be...'. Dramática is the girl form; to a boy it's dramático. Also heard: ¡No exageres!
Tómate = 'take' (for medicine, food or drink). In Spain you say un paracetamol, meaning one tablet.

phrases.en: Do you need to see the doctor?
phrases.note: Hace falta = 'is it needed'. Very common in Spain: No hace falta = 'no need'. El médico = the doctor.

phrases.ph: ah pah-SAH-doh AHL-goh ehn ehl eens-tee-TOO-toh
phrases.note: El instituto (or el insti) is secondary school in Spain. ¿Ha pasado algo? = 'has something happened?'

phrases.en: Go and lie down for a bit.
phrases.note: Tumbarse = 'to lie down'. Un rato = 'a little while' — you'll hear rato all the time in Spain.
Arder = 'to burn'. Said with a hand on your forehead when you've got a temperature.
Suficiente = 'enough'. Agua is feminine but uses el: el agua fría.

phrases.en: It's not the end of the world.
phrases.es: No es el fin del mundo.
phrases.ph: noh ehs ehl feen dehl MOON-doh
phrases.note: El fin del mundo = 'the end of the world'. Same idea as English — great for calming someone down.
The go-to phrase for feeling unwell. When you're better, just swap mal for bien: me encuentro bien.
Literally 'the head hurts me'. Spanish uses la (the), not 'my', for body parts. Swap cabeza for any body part: me duele el pie (my foot hurts).
Tripa is the everyday word for tummy in Spain. Estómago works too, but tripa is what you'd say at home.
Garganta means throat — think of 'gargle'. Same 'me duele' pattern as for a headache.

phrases.en: I think I've got a temperature.
phrases.note: Fiebre means fever. Spanish says 'I have fever' (tengo fiebre), with no 'a'. Creo que = 'I think that'.
Preocupada por = 'worried about'. A boy says preocupado. In exámenes the stress falls on the accented á.
Agobiada means stressed or overwhelmed — very common in Spain. Estresada also works. A boy says agobiado.
Abrazo is a hug; abrazar is 'to hug'. In Spain the z is said like the 'th' in 'think'.
Estoy harta = 'I'm fed up'. Harta is for a girl — a boy says harto. Add de + thing: harta de la tele.
Said with a sulky face, estoy bien means the opposite — just like in English. Tone does all the work.
Déjame en paz = literally 'leave me in peace'. Sounds sharp — fine with family, rude with anyone else.
Nadie = 'nobody'. Me entiende = 'understands me'. Peak teen drama, works just as well in Spanish.
Tengo ganas de... = 'I feel like...'. Vomitar = to be sick. Also: Tengo el estómago revuelto (upset stomach).
Me está matando = 'is killing me'. Swap the body part: los pies me están matando (my feet are killing me).
La regla = 'period' in Spain. Tengo dolor de... = 'I've got pain in/from...'. You can also say me ha bajado la regla.
Agobio = that stressed, overwhelmed feeling. Very Spanish. Estoy agobiada is the girl form; a boy says agobiado.
Qué + noun = 'what a...!'. Aburrimiento = boredom. Or say Me aburro = 'I'm bored'.
De mal humor = 'in a bad mood'. Humor here means mood, not jokes. Happy version: de buen humor.
Solo = 'just' or 'only'. Solo quiero... is a handy start: solo quiero estar tranquila.
Me muero de... = 'I'm dying of...'. Works with lots: me muero de sueño (so sleepy), me muero de frío.
No estoy de humor = 'I'm not in the mood'. Add para + thing: no estoy de humor para bromas (for jokes).

phrases.en: It's been the worst day ever.
phrases.es: Ha sido el peor día de mi vida.
phrases.ph: ah SEE-doh ehl peh-OHR DEE-ah deh mee BEE-dah
phrases.note: El peor día de mi vida = 'the worst day of my life'. Spanish uses 'of my life' where English says 'ever'.
Estoy muerta = 'I'm dead', meaning exhausted. A boy says muerto. Also: estoy reventada.
Exagerar = 'to exaggerate' or overreact. Your comeback when someone says you're being dramatic.

phrases.en: I don't want to talk about it.
phrases.note: El tema = 'the subject'. Del = de + el. You'll also hear: Paso del tema (I'm not getting into it).

phrases.en: I think I'm getting a cold.
phrases.note: Resfriarse = 'to catch a cold'. A cold is un resfriado or, very commonly in Spain, un constipado.
Orgulloso is for a dad saying it — mum says orgullosa. Proud 'of' you is de ti.
From rendirse (to give up or surrender). The r at the start of a word is rolled strongly.
Just 'you can' — Spanish doesn't need the 'do it'. Adding tú makes it more encouraging: YOU can.
Literally 'lots of luck'. Just ¡Suerte! is fine too, e.g. before an exam.
Quedar here means 'to turn out', so it's 'it's turned out great for you'. Perfect for artwork, cooking or homework.
Gracias por + verb = 'thanks for doing something'. Try gracias por esperar (thanks for waiting).
Te quiero is how family and friends say 'I love you'. Te amo is much more romantic, so keep that for partners.
Guapa means pretty, and -ísima makes it 'really'. To a boy: estás guapísimo.
Sigue is from seguir (to carry on) and así means 'like this'. The u in sigue is silent — it just keeps the g hard.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter if you get it wrong.
phrases.es: No pasa nada si te equivocas.
phrases.ph: noh PAH-sah NAH-dah see teh eh-kee-BOH-kahs
phrases.note: Equivocarse means 'to make a mistake'. No pasa nada ('nothing happens') is a very Spanish way to say 'it's fine'.
Literally 'do what you can'. Haz is the command form of hacer (to do).
A handy pattern: se me da bien = I'm good at it, se te da bien = you're good at it. Add a verb: se te da bien dibujar.
Use this for achievements like passing an exam. For birthdays, say ¡Felicidades! instead. The h is silent.
Maja is a very Spain word for nice or kind. Say majo to a boy. Qué + describing word = 'how...!'
Bien hecho = 'well done'. You can also hear ¡Muy bien! for a quick 'good job'.

phrases.en: I knew you could do it.
phrases.note: Sabía = 'I knew'. Podías = 'you could'. No need to add 'do it' in Spanish — it's understood.
Menuda = 'what a...!' — works for good or bad: ¡menudo día! (what a day!). Nota = mark.
Esforzarse = 'to make an effort'. Praising effort, not just results — tu esfuerzo = your effort.
Genial = 'brilliant' or 'great'. Short, easy and used by everyone, all the time.

phrases.es: No pasa nada, otra vez será.
phrases.ph: noh PAH-sah NAH-dah, OH-trah behth seh-RAH
phrases.note: Otra vez será = 'it'll happen another time'. The go-to line for cheering someone up after a let-down.
He hecho = 'I have done', from hacer. Both h's are silent — Spanish never pronounces h.
Conseguir means 'to manage' or 'to achieve'. Great to shout when you finally do something hard.
La mejor is for mum. To dad, say eres el mejor. The j is a throaty sound, like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'.
Sacar una nota = 'to get a mark'. Sacar is the verb Spanish students always use for grades.
Se me da bien = 'I'm good at it'. Pattern: se me da mal = I'm bad at it; se te da bien = you're good at it.
Mamá has the accent on the last a. Swap in papá for Dad — same accent.
Te lo dije = 'I told you so'. Sounds smug — which is kind of the point.

phrases.es: Estoy muy orgullosa de mí misma.
phrases.ph: ehs-TOY mwee ohr-goo-YOH-sah deh mee MEES-mah
phrases.note: Orgullosa and misma are girl forms; a boy says orgulloso de mí mismo. Mí with an accent means 'me'.
Increíble = 'amazing' or 'unbelievable'. Also very common: ¡Qué pasada! (Spain slang for 'how awesome').
Bien hecho = 'well done' (literally 'well made'). Works for anyone — not for steak, though!
No está mal = 'not bad'. Can be a real compliment or a cheeky, grudging one — depends on your tone.
Clavar = 'to nail'. Lo he clavado = 'I nailed it'. Same image as English, used by Spanish teens too.
In Spain marks go from 0 to 10, so un diez is top marks. Un cinco is a pass.
Aprobar = 'to pass' (an exam). The opposite is suspender = to fail — a word you'll hear a lot in Spain.
Guay = 'cool' in Spain. Very common with teens. ¡Qué guay! = 'how cool!'
Di is the short command from decir (to say). Por favor literally means 'as a favour'.
Spanish says 'give the thanks' (dar las gracias), not 'say thank you'. Da is the command form of dar (to give).
The classic parent prompt — literally 'what is said?'. The expected answer is 'gracias' or 'por favor'.
Literally 'of nothing' — as in 'it was nothing'. The standard reply to gracias.
Literally 'nothing happens'. Perfect reply when someone says sorry for something small.
What Spanish people say after a sneeze. ¡Salud! (health) works too. The J is a throaty sound, like the 'ch' in 'loch'.
Use perdona to get someone's attention or get past them. With a stranger or older person, say perdone instead — it's more polite.
Llamar means 'to knock' here, but also 'to call' (on the phone). Antes de + verb = 'before doing'.

phrases.es: Eso ha sido de mala educación.
phrases.ph: EH-soh ah SEE-doh deh MAH-lah eh-doo-kah-THYOHN
phrases.note: Educación here means manners, not school education. Mala educación = bad manners. Sounds firm.
Cariño means 'love' or 'darling' and stays the same for a boy or a girl. The ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon'.
No interrumpas = 'don't interrupt'. Also heard: ¡No cortes! (don't cut in).
Pedir perdón = 'to say sorry' (literally 'ask for forgiveness'). Pídele = ask him.

phrases.en: Say it like you mean it.
phrases.note: Lo siento = I'm sorry; como si lo sintieras = as if you felt it. For a sulky, mumbled apology.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.es: No hables con la boca llena.
phrases.ph: noh AH-blehs kohn lah BOH-kah YEH-nah
phrases.note: La boca llena = 'your mouth full'. Spanish says 'the mouth', not 'your mouth', for body parts.

phrases.en: Don't speak to me like that.
phrases.note: Así = 'like that'. Short and firm — the classic parent warning.
Cuidado con... = 'careful with...'. Ese tono = that tone. Reuse it: cuidado con el perro.
Saludar = 'to say hello'. In Spain that often means two kisses on the cheeks for family.
Modales = 'manners'. ¿Y esos...? = 'and what about those...?' — a telling-off in question form.
Goes at the start or end of a request: ¿me ayudas, por favor? Literally 'as a favour'.
In Spain the c in gracias is said like 'th'; in Latin America it's an s. Both are understood everywhere.
Muchas has an -as ending to match gracias. Never say 'mucho gracias'.
Literally 'I feel it'. Use it for a real apology. For bumping into someone, just say ¡perdón!

phrases.en: Excuse me, can I get past?
phrases.note: Pasar means 'to go through' or 'come in'. ¿Se puede pasar? is what you'd say knocking on a door.
La cena is the evening meal. Lunch is la comida, and breakfast is el desayuno.
Querer means both 'to want' and 'to love'. With te before it, it's love. Mamá has the stress on the last syllable.
También means 'too' or 'also'. Just 'y yo a ti' ('and me to you') works as a quick reply too.
Means 'relax, it's fine'. Say tranquila to Mum and tranquilo to Dad — it matches the person you're talking to.
Perdón = 'sorry'. Adding ¿vale? makes it sound sulky and impatient — just like 'OK?' in English.
Ya = 'already'. Ya te he pedido perdón = 'I've already said sorry to you'. Handy when they won't let it go.

phrases.en: Sorry, can I just say something?
phrases.note: Perdona = 'excuse me' to one person you know. Una cosa = 'one thing' — used like 'something' here.
Llamar = 'to knock' here, but it also means 'to call'. Antes = 'first' or 'before'.

phrases.en: Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.
phrases.es: Perdona, no lo he hecho aposta.
phrases.ph: pehr-DOH-nah, noh loh eh EH-choh ah-POHS-tah
phrases.note: Aposta = 'on purpose' — very Spain. Elsewhere people say a propósito, which is understood too.
Interrumpir = 'to interrupt'. Me has... = 'you have ... me'. Good comeback when it's your turn to talk.
Traerme = 'bringing me'. Spain has no single word for 'lift' — you say thanks for bringing/taking me (llevarme).

phrases.en: Can I leave the table, please?
phrases.es: ¿Puedo levantarme de la mesa, por favor?
phrases.ph: PWEH-doh leh-bahn-TAHR-meh deh lah MEH-sah, pohr fah-BOHR
phrases.note: Levantarse = 'to get up'. Spanish says 'get up from the table' rather than 'leave'.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: Echar una mano = 'to give a hand'. Very common in Spain for any small job, from shopping bags to cooking.
La compra = 'the food shopping'. For clothes shopping you'd say ir de compras instead.
Sujetar = 'to hold (still)'. The me means 'for me' — handy with any favour: ¿me sujetas esto?
Spanish just says 'open the door' when someone knocks or rings. Abrir = to open.
Ayuda = 'help' (the noun). The verb is ayudar: ¿te ayudo? = 'shall I help you?'
Spanish uses the plain present for offers: ¿te ayudo? = 'shall I help you?' Same trick: ¿te lo llevo? = 'shall I carry it?'
Literally 'leave it to me'. Say it with a sigh when someone is making a mess of a job.
Trae = 'give it here' (from traer, to bring). Que lo hago yo = 'I'll do it'. A bit impatient!
Enseñar means both 'to show' and 'to teach'. Enséñamelo = show + me + it, all stuck together.
Coger = 'to grab/take' — totally normal in Spain, but avoid it in Latin America, where it's rude.
Pasar = 'to pass'. Add me on the end for 'pass me': pásame el mando = 'pass me the remote'.
¿Qué te pasa? = 'what's up with you?' Gentle if said kindly — sharp if said with a frown.
Gafas = 'glasses' — always plural in Spanish. Gafas de sol = sunglasses.
Llaves = 'keys'. Swap in anything: ¿has visto mi móvil? = 'have you seen my phone?'
Buscar = 'to look for / search'. Buscarlo en internet = 'look it up online'.
Ayúdame a + verb = 'help me (do something)'. Ayúdame a poner la mesa = 'help me lay the table'.

phrases.en: Can you set this up for me?
phrases.note: Configurar = 'to set up' a phone, app or TV. Classic parent-to-teen request!

phrases.en: I could do with some help here.
phrases.es: No me vendría mal una ayudita.
phrases.ph: noh meh behn-DREE-ah mahl OO-nah ah-yoo-DEE-tah
phrases.note: Ayudita = 'a little help'. Adding -ita makes a word small and softer — a polite hint.
Handy pattern: ¿Me puedes + verb? = 'Can you ... me?' You can also say ¿Puedes ayudarme? — same meaning.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Con esto = 'with this'. Swap in anything: con los deberes (with my homework).

phrases.en: Can you do this for me?
phrases.note: Por mí here means 'for me' in the sense of 'instead of me'. Mí needs its accent when it means 'me'.
Abrir is 'to open'; the opposite is cerrar, 'to close'. Great for jars and stubborn packets.
Llegar usually means 'to arrive', but ¿Llegas? also means 'can you reach?' Ahí = 'there' — point at the high shelf.
Arreglar means 'to fix' or 'sort out'. The double rr is a rolled r — give it a little trill.
Mirar means 'to look at' — the 'at' is built in, so don't add a. ¡Mira! on its own means 'Look!'
Revisar is 'to check' or 'look over' — ideal for homework. It's not 'revise' for exams; that's repasar.
No word for 'do' in the question part — Spanish just says 'how I-do this?' Hago = 'I do', with a silent h.
Significa = 'it means'. Super useful for Spanish homework: ¿Qué significa esta palabra? (this word).
Ir (to go) is used for where things belong, just like English. For a jigsaw or flat-pack, point and ask ¿Dónde va?
Enseñar means both 'to show' and 'to teach'. The ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon'.
Venir already means 'come (here)', so aquí is optional. Much politer than the parent-style ¡Ven aquí!
Sujetar means 'to hold (steady)'. The j is the throaty sound you hear in 'loch' — not an English j.
Llevar covers 'carry', 'take' and even 'wear'. Here it means carrying something for you.

phrases.en: Can you get this for me?
phrases.note: Traer means 'to bring' (towards you). Its opposite is llevar, 'to take' away.
The lo ('it') is tacked onto the end of encontrar. Use encontrarla if the lost thing is feminine, like la llave.
Visto means 'seen' — an odd one, from ver. Lo = 'it'; say ¿La has visto? for a feminine thing.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: Echar una mano is exactly like English 'give a hand'. Echar usually means 'to throw'.
Atascado means 'stuck' or 'jammed' — lids, zips, doors. Use atascada for feminine things like la puerta.
Roto comes from romper, 'to break'. Roll the r at the start. La silla está rota for feminine things.
Funcionar = 'to work' for machines. For people working, use trabajar instead.
No me sale literally means 'it doesn't come out for me' — what Spanish speakers say when a task or sum just won't work.

phrases.ph: meh loh PWEH-dehs ehks-plee-KAHR OH-trah behth
phrases.note: Otra vez = 'again' (literally 'another time'). Explicar is 'to explain' — the x sounds like 'ks', and there's no 'ay' sound.
Spanish says 'I've done myself harm'. Daño = 'harm' or 'hurt' — the ñ sounds like 'ny'.
Spanish says el dedo ('the finger'), not 'my finger' — the me already shows it's yours. Same with me duele la cabeza.
El tuyo = 'yours'. It changes with the thing: la tuya for feminine words like la chaqueta.

phrases.en: I don't know how it works.
phrases.note: No sé cómo... = 'I don't know how...'. Keep the accent on sé — without it, se means something else.
Literally 'it weighs a lot' — from pesar, 'to weigh'. This is the everyday way to say something is too heavy.

phrases.es: El dinero no crece en los árboles.
phrases.ph: ehl dee-NEH-roh noh KREH-theh ehn lohs AHR-boh-lehs
phrases.note: Same saying as in English. Crecer = 'to grow', árboles = 'trees'.

phrases.en: What do you need it for?
phrases.note: ¿Para qué? = 'what for?' On its own it's a great short reply: ¿Para qué?
Demasiado = 'too (much)'. Caro = 'expensive'; for a feminine thing, cara: la chaqueta es demasiado cara.
Costar = 'to cost'. For more than one thing: ¿cuánto cuestan?
Pagar = 'to pay'. Págalo = 'pay for it'. Tu dinero = 'your money'.

phrases.en: You've already spent your pocket money.
phrases.es: Ya te has gastado la paga.
phrases.ph: yah teh ahs gahs-TAH-doh lah PAH-gah
phrases.note: La paga = 'pocket money' in Spain. Gastar = 'to spend' (money, not time).
La mitad = 'half'. Spanish often uses the present for promises: te doy = 'I'll give you'.

phrases.en: Put it on your birthday list.
phrases.note: Pídelo = 'ask for it'. Para Reyes works too — in Spain the Three Kings bring presents on 6 January.
Putting eso first makes it firmer: 'THAT, we're not buying'. End of discussion.
Suelto = 'loose change' in Spain. El cambio is the change you get back after paying.
Literally 'it's throwing money away'. Tirar = 'to throw (away)'.
Mandar = 'to send'. Te lo = 'it to you'. In Spain people often send money by Bizum, an app.
Hacer falta = 'to be needed'. No te hace falta = 'you don't need it' — very common in Spain.

phrases.en: What happened to your birthday money?
phrases.es: ¿Qué has hecho con el dinero de tu cumpleaños?
phrases.ph: keh ahs EH-choh kohn ehl dee-NEH-roh deh too koom-pleh-AH-nyohs
phrases.note: Literally 'what have you done with…?' Hecho comes from hacer, to do.
Ahorrar = 'to save (money)'. Tendrás que = 'you'll have to' — useful for all sorts of nagging.

phrases.en: Do I look like a bank?
phrases.ph: TEHN-goh KAH-rah deh BAHN-koh oh keh
phrases.note: Tener cara de = 'to look like'. Sarcastic — o qué on the end adds attitude.
Spanish often puts no at the end for a short, firm answer: hoy no = 'not today'.

phrases.en: You'll have to pay me back.
phrases.note: Devolver = 'to give back / pay back'. Also used for returning things to a shop.
Las rebajas = 'the sales'. In Spain the big ones start in January and July.

phrases.en: Do you think I'm made of money?
phrases.note: Millonario = 'millionaire'; a mum says millonaria. Te crees que… = 'do you really think…'.
Literally 'will you give me money?' ¿Me das...? is the everyday way to ask for something. Spanish doesn't need a word for 'some'.

phrases.en: Can you send me some money?
phrases.note: Mandar means 'to send' — you can use it for money, messages or photos: mándame la foto, 'send me the photo'.
Spanish flips it round: ¿Me prestas...? means 'will you lend me...?' Use it for anything — ¿Me prestas tu cargador?
Devolver means 'to give back'. Te lo devuelvo = 'I give it back to you' — works for money or anything you've borrowed.
Esto means 'this' for a thing you're pointing at when you don't name it. Comprar is 'to buy'.

phrases.en: Can you buy this for me?
phrases.note: The little me does the job of 'for me' — no need for para mí. Compare ¿Puedo comprar esto? (Can I buy this?).
Pedir means 'to order' (online or in a café) and also 'to ask for'. Algo = 'something'.
Tarjeta is 'card' — bank card, gift card or birthday card. The j is a throaty sound, like the ch in 'loch'.
Literally 'how much does it cost?' — from costar. For more than one thing, say ¿Cuánto cuestan?
Libras = 'pounds' (money); in Spain you'd be talking in euros. Solo means 'only' here.
De oferta = 'on offer/on sale'. For the big seasonal sales, Spain says las rebajas.
Lo means 'it' and goes before the verb. If the thing is feminine, like la chaqueta, say la necesito.
Todo el mundo means 'everyone' — literally 'all the world'. Use una instead of uno if the thing is feminine.
Ir de compras = 'go shopping' for fun. For food shopping Spain says hacer la compra.
In Spain 'town' in this sense is el centro, the town centre. Al is a + el squashed together.

phrases.en: Can you take me to the shops?
phrases.ph: meh PWEH-dehs yeh-BAHR ah lahs TYEHN-dahs
phrases.note: Tienda means 'shop'. Swap in any place after a: ¿Me puedes llevar al centro comercial? (to the shopping centre).

phrases.en: I don't have any money left.
phrases.note: Quedar here means 'to be left'. No me queda = 'there isn't any left for me' — same as no me queda batería.

phrases.en: Can I have my pocket money?
phrases.note: La paga is what kids in Spain call pocket money. ¿Me das...? is the easy way to ask for anything.
Ahorrar means 'to save' money. The h is silent and the double rr is rolled.
Demasiado = 'too' (too much). Caro is 'expensive' — use cara for a feminine thing, like la chaqueta es demasiado cara.
Barato = 'cheap', the opposite of caro. Becomes barata for feminine things: la camiseta es muy barata.

phrases.en: I want to buy her a present.
phrases.note: The -le on comprarle means 'for her' (or 'for him'). Regalo is 'present' or 'gift'.

phrases.en: Can I use my birthday money?
phrases.es: ¿Puedo usar el dinero de mi cumpleaños?
phrases.ph: PWEH-doh oo-SAHR ehl dee-NEH-roh deh mee koom-pleh-AH-nyohs
phrases.note: Spanish says 'the money of my birthday' — el dinero de mi cumpleaños. Same pattern for la paga de la semana.
Gastar means 'to spend' money. The extra me adds a 'yep, all of it' feeling that Spanish speakers love.

phrases.en: Can you lend me ten pounds?
phrases.note: Prestar = 'to lend', so this is literally 'will you lend me ten pounds?' In Spain, the z in diez sounds like 'th'.
A set phrase in Spain — literally 'it deserves the pain'. The opposite is no merece la pena.
El cambio is 'the change' from paying. Quedarse + thing means 'to keep' it.
El cinturón = 'belt'; in a car everyone knows it means the seatbelt. Ponte = 'put on'.

phrases.es: Deja de dar patadas al asiento.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh dahr pah-TAH-dahs ahl ah-SYEHN-toh
phrases.note: Deja de + verb = 'stop doing'. Dar patadas = 'to kick' (literally 'give kicks').
Guardar = 'to put away / keep'. El móvil is the Spain word for mobile phone.
Ya casi = 'nearly now'. The answer to every ¿ya hemos llegado?
Quedar = 'to be left'. Queda poco = 'there's not much left' — works for time, food or battery.

phrases.en: Go to the toilet before we leave.
phrases.es: Ve al baño antes de salir.
phrases.ph: beh ahl BAH-nyoh AHN-tehs deh sah-LEER
phrases.note: Antes de + verb = 'before doing'. In Spain el baño is the normal word for toilet at home.
Hagáis is the vosotros form — talking to both kids at once. To one person: no hagas tanto ruido.
Intentar = 'to try'. Concentrarme = 'to concentrate' — the me on the end means 'myself'.
Distraer = 'to distract'. Said sharply — a driver means it!

phrases.en: Who's in charge of the music?
phrases.note: Poner música = 'to put music on'. Spanish has no word like 'aux' — just ask who's putting it on.
Otra vez = 'again'. Put no at the end for a proper groan.

phrases.es: Coge tus cosas, que ya hemos llegado.
phrases.ph: KOH-heh toos KOH-sahs, keh yah EH-mohs yeh-GAH-doh
phrases.note: Tus cosas = 'your stuff'. Que here just means 'because' — very common in spoken Spanish.
Te espero = 'I'll wait for you'. El coche is the Spain word — in Latin America it's often carro or auto.

phrases.en: Are you getting out or not?
phrases.note: Bajarse = 'to get out' of a car or bus. Subirse = 'to get in'. O qué adds impatience.
Subir = 'to go up', but also 'to get into' a car, bus or train.

phrases.en: Hurry up, I'm in the car.
phrases.es: Date prisa, que estoy en el coche.
phrases.ph: DAH-teh PREE-sah, keh ehs-TOY ehn ehl KOH-cheh
phrases.note: Darse prisa = 'to hurry'. Date prisa = 'hurry up' to one person; to both kids: daos prisa.
Dejad is the vosotros form — to both kids. Ahí detrás = 'back there'.
No comas = 'don't eat'. The verb changes after no when giving an order: come → no comas.

phrases.en: If you feel sick, tell me.
phrases.note: Marearse = 'to feel carsick/dizzy'. Avísame = 'let me know' — really useful word.
In a car the window is la ventanilla, not la ventana. The -illa makes it 'little window'.
Dejar = 'to leave / drop off'. Te recojo a las diez = 'I'll pick you up at ten'.
Bajar = 'to turn down' (volume). Súbelo = 'turn it up'.
Literally 'Have we arrived already?' Llegar means 'to arrive' — in Spain the ll sounds like an English y.
Faltar means 'to be missing/still to go'. ¿Cuánto falta? is the Spanish kid's classic car question — much more natural than using 'left'.
Vamos a tardar = 'we're going to take'. Spanish talks about how long we take, rather than 'it'.
Vamos is 'we go' — and also 'let's go!' on its own. Adónde asks 'where to?'

phrases.en: Can I sit in the front?
phrases.note: Spanish says 'Can I go in front?' — ir delante. The back seat is detrás: Yo voy detrás.

phrases.en: Can you turn the music up?
phrases.note: Subir means 'to go up/raise', so subir la música is 'raise the music'. Handy pattern: ¿Puedes + verb? = 'Can you...?'
Bajar is the opposite of subir: 'to lower'. The lo stuck on the end means 'it' (el volumen); for la música say bajarla.
Elegir means 'to choose'. A g before i or e is the throaty 'loch' sound, not a hard g. Puedo = 'can I'.
Parar means 'to stop' (the same verb as ¡Para!). On a motorway in Spain you'd stop at an área de servicio.
Spanish says 'I need to go to the bathroom'. Baño is the polite everyday word; al is a + el squashed together.
Spanish says 'I have hunger' — tengo hambre. Don't say estoy hambre. Tengo mucha hambre = 'I'm really hungry'.
Like hunger, thirst is something you 'have': tengo sed. Sed is a tiny word — the d at the end is very soft.
Cansada is for a girl — your brother would say estoy cansado. Estoy is used because tiredness is a passing state.
You 'have cold' in Spanish — tengo frío. Estoy fría would mean your body is cold to touch, so avoid it.
Always say tengo calor for feeling hot. Estoy caliente has an embarrassing other meaning — best avoided!

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating on?
phrases.note: Poner ('to put') is used for switching things on: poner la calefacción, poner la tele. To turn off, use quitar or apagar.

phrases.en: Can you turn the air conditioning on?
phrases.note: People in Spain often shorten it to just el aire: ¿Pones el aire? Same poner pattern as the heating.
Ventana is a window in a house or car. Opposite: ¿Puedes cerrar la ventana? ('close'). In a car you could also say bajar la ventanilla.
Volver means 'to go back/return'. A casa means 'home' when you're heading there — no word for 'the' needed.
Marearse means 'to get travel-sick or dizzy' — from mar, the sea. Estoy mareada (a boy: mareado) means 'I feel sick'.
Spanish says el móvil ('the mobile') rather than 'my' when it's obvious whose it is. Móvil is the Spain word — not celular.

phrases.en: Can I put my headphones in?
phrases.note: Cascos (literally 'helmets') is the everyday Spain word for headphones. Ponerse = 'to put on yourself', hence the me.

phrases.es: Me está dando patadas al asiento.
phrases.ph: meh ehs-TAH DAHN-doh pah-TAH-dahs ahl ah-SYEHN-toh
phrases.note: Dar patadas is 'to give kicks' — Spanish usually says it this way rather than one verb. Asiento means 'seat'.
Hay (h silent, sounds like English 'eye') means 'there is/are'. A traffic jam is un atasco: Hay un atasco.
Estamos is 'we are' from estar, the verb for location. Same pattern as ¿Dónde estás? but for 'we'.

phrases.en: Can you pass me my bag?
phrases.note: ¿Me pasas...? ('Do you pass me...?') is a friendly way to ask for things — works at the table too. Mochila is a rucksack.
Viene is 'is coming' from venir. Spanish often puts the verb first in questions: ¿Viene Monty? — no extra word needed.
Carretera is a road between towns; a street in town is la calle. Roll the rr in the middle strongly.
Spanish uses hace (it makes) for lots of weather: hace sol, hace frío, hace calor, hace viento.
A fun Spain saying — literally 'it's a cold that peels (your skin)'. Hace mucho frío is the plain version.
Paraguas is 'stops-waters' (para + aguas), and it keeps its s even for one umbrella. Llévate = take it with you.
Viento is wind. Muchísimo is a bigger version of mucho — 'loads of'.
Ponte means 'put on yourself' and works for clothes too: ponte el abrigo (put your coat on).
Va a + verb = 'it's going to...'. Llover is 'to rain'; está lloviendo means 'it's raining'.
From abrigarse, 'to wrap up'. It's linked to abrigo, the word for a coat.
Calor is heat, so this is 'today it makes a lot of heat'. Don't say 'es caliente' for the weather — that sounds wrong.
Literally 'there's ice outside'. The h in hielo is silent, so it starts with a y-like sound.
Nevando comes from nevar (to snow) — like Sierra Nevada, the 'snowy mountains'. Nieve is snow.
Tormenta is a storm, especially with thunder. Viene means 'is coming', from venir.

phrases.en: Bring the washing in, it's raining.
phrases.es: Recoge la ropa, que está lloviendo.
phrases.ph: rreh-KOH-heh lah RROH-pah, keh ehs-TAH yoh-BYEHN-doh
phrases.note: Recoger means to bring in or pick up. La ropa is clothes, and here it means the washing on the line.
Abrigo = 'coat'. Abrigarse means 'to wrap up warm', so you'll hear the same word a lot in winter.
Ponte = 'put on (yourself)'. Spanish uses el abrigo, not 'your coat', because it's obvious whose it is.

phrases.en: You're not going out like that, it's freezing.
phrases.es: Así no sales, que hace un frío que pela.
phrases.ph: ah-SEE noh SAH-lehs, keh AH-theh oon FREE-oh keh PEH-lah
phrases.note: Hace un frío que pela is a very Spanish way to say 'it's freezing' — literally 'a cold that peels'. Así = 'like that'.
Quítate = 'take off (yourself)', the opposite of ponte. Mojado = 'wet'; the -s is there because zapatos is plural.

phrases.en: Shut the door, you're letting the cold in.
phrases.es: Cierra la puerta, que entra frío.
phrases.ph: THYEH-rrah lah PWEHR-tah, keh EHN-trah FREE-oh
phrases.note: That little que at the start of the reason means 'because' — parents in Spain add it to almost every nag.

phrases.en: It's only a bit of rain.
phrases.note: Cuatro gotas = literally 'four drops'. Spaniards use it to mean 'hardly any rain' — say it when someone's making a fuss.
Hace calor = 'it's hot' (weather). For how you feel, it's tengo calor — never estoy caliente, which sounds rude!
Resfriarse = 'to catch a cold'; un resfriado is 'a cold'. Vas a + verb is the easy way to talk about the future.
Only three words! Just raise your voice at the end to make it a question.
Tiempo means both 'weather' and 'time'. Here it's 'what weather does it make?'.
Abrigo is a proper coat; a light jacket is una chaqueta. Spanish often drops the 'a' here.
Empapada means soaked through — a boy says empapado. Good for coming in from the rain.
Qué + a noun = 'what a...!' or 'so much...!'. So this is 'what heat!'. Try ¡qué frío! too.
Literally 'I'm dying of cold' — Spanish loves a bit of drama. Works for hunger too: me muero de hambre.

phrases.en: What's the weather going to be like tomorrow?
phrases.ph: keh TYEHM-poh bah ah ah-THEHR mah-NYAH-nah
phrases.note: Same as ¿qué tiempo hace? but with va a hacer for 'going to be'. Mañana means tomorrow (and also morning).

phrases.es: Aquí dentro hace un frío que pela.
phrases.ph: ah-KEE DEHN-troh AH-theh oon FREE-oh keh PEH-lah
phrases.note: Aquí dentro = 'in here'. Add it to a weather phrase to complain about the house rather than outside.
No pienso + verb = 'I'm not going to, and that's that'. Sounds stubborn — perfect for arguing.
Asarse = 'to roast'. Me estoy asando is the everyday Spanish for 'I'm boiling'.
Empapado = 'soaked'. Spanish says 'I have the shoes soaked' — tengo + thing + describing word is a handy pattern.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating up?
phrases.note: Subir = 'turn up' and bajar = 'turn down'. Works for the volume too: sube la música.
Odio = 'I hate'. La lluvia is 'the rain'; the verb 'to rain' is llover.

phrases.en: Can we go to the beach?
phrases.note: Playa = 'beach'. Remember a + la stays a la, but a + el becomes al: al parque.
Nevar = 'to snow', and la nieve is 'snow'. Está + -ando means it's happening right now.
In Spanish you 'have' cold: tengo frío. The go-to reply when a parent says ponte el abrigo.

phrases.en: Can you put the air con on?
phrases.note: El aire is short for el aire acondicionado — in Spain everyone just says el aire.
Otra vez = 'again'. Uf is the Spanish 'ugh' — sighing sound included.
Fatal = 'awful' in Spain, not 'deadly'. Estoy fatal = 'I feel awful'.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift? It's pouring.
phrases.note: ¿Me llevas? = 'will you take me?' — the normal way to ask for a lift. Diluviar comes from diluvio, 'flood'.

phrases.en: What do you want to do this weekend?
phrases.es: ¿Qué quieres hacer este fin de semana?
phrases.ph: keh KYEH-rehs ah-THEHR EHS-teh feen deh seh-MAH-nah
phrases.note: Fin de semana is literally 'end of week'. ¿Qué quieres + verb? = 'What do you want to...?'.
Using the 'we' form as a question (¿jugamos?) is how you say 'shall we...?'. Jugar needs a after it: jugar a algo.
Vamos a + verb = 'let's...'. Dar un paseo is literally 'give a walk' — that's just how Spanish says it.

phrases.en: Shall we watch a film tonight?
phrases.note: Peli is short for película (film) and everyone in Spain uses it. Esta noche = tonight.
Pedir means 'to order' or 'to ask for'. Spanish often uses the present tense for plans, like English 'we're ordering'.

phrases.en: We're going to Grandma's on Sunday.
phrases.es: El domingo vamos a casa de la abuela.
phrases.ph: ehl doh-MEEN-goh BAH-mohs ah KAH-sah deh lah ah-BWEH-lah
phrases.note: There's no 's for 'Grandma's' — you say 'to the house of the grandma'. El domingo = on Sunday, with no word for 'on'.

phrases.en: Do you want to come with us?
phrases.note: Nosotros means 'us' here. If everyone going is female, it becomes nosotras.
Prisa means hurry. You'll also hear date prisa — 'hurry up'.
Ganar means 'to win' (and 'to earn'). Va ganando is like 'is going along winning'.
Tocar usually means 'to touch', but te toca means 'it's your turn'. Me toca = my turn!
Salir = 'to go out'. Vamos a + verb = 'we're going to'; on its own ¡vamos! means 'come on!'.
Ponte = 'put on'. Swap in any clothes: ponte la chaqueta, ponte las zapatillas (trainers).
Toca = 'it's time for'. Ahora toca + activity is a very Spanish way to announce what's next: ahora toca cenar.

phrases.es: Vamos a ver a la abuela.
phrases.ph: BAH-mohs ah behr ah lah ah-BWEH-lah
phrases.note: Notice the little a before la abuela — Spanish adds it when the thing you see is a person.

phrases.en: Turn that off and come outside.
phrases.note: Apaga = 'turn off', sal = 'go out' (from salir). Eso = 'that', handy when you don't know what gadget it is.

phrases.en: You're coming whether you like it or not.
phrases.note: Quieras o no = 'whether you like it or not'. Classic parent line — no arguing after this one.

phrases.en: Some fresh air will do you good.
phrases.es: Te vendrá bien que te dé el aire.
phrases.ph: teh behn-DRAH byehn keh teh deh ehl EYE-reh
phrases.note: Te vendrá bien = 'it'll do you good'. Que te dé el aire = literally 'for the air to hit you'.

phrases.en: You can't spend all day in bed.
phrases.es: No puedes pasarte el día en la cama.
phrases.ph: noh PWEH-dehs pah-SAHR-teh ehl DEE-ah ehn lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Pasarse el día + place/doing = 'to spend all day'. Also: te pasas el día con el móvil.
Casi = 'nearly'. The que at the start adds a 'honestly!' feel — it's a telling-off, not just the time.

phrases.es: Deja de quejarte, que va a ser divertido.
phrases.ph: DEH-hah deh keh-HAHR-teh, keh bah ah sehr dee-behr-TEE-doh
phrases.note: Deja de + verb = 'stop doing'. Quejarse = 'to moan'. Deja de gritar, deja de cantar — same pattern.
Literally 'brighten that face'. Esa cara (that face) makes it a bit teasing.
Pues here means 'well, then'. Aburrida is for a girl — to the brother it's ¿aburrido?
Just two words — the 'we' form of ver (to watch) does all the work. In Spanish a v sounds just like a soft b.
¿Podemos + verb? = 'Can we...?'. A series is una serie.

phrases.es: ¿Podemos ir a casa de la abuela?
phrases.ph: poh-DEH-mohs eer ah KAH-sah deh lah ah-BWEH-lah
phrases.note: Abuela is grandma and abuelo is grandad. Informally you might also hear la yaya.
Palomitas literally means 'little doves' — the popped corn is meant to look like them.

phrases.en: I don't want to watch that.
phrases.note: No quiero + verb = 'I don't want to...'. Eso means 'that'.
Elegir means 'to choose' — think 'elect'. A g before i or e is the throaty sound, like the 'ch' in 'loch'.

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Al is a + el squashed together ('to the'). In Spain, the c in cine is a 'th' sound.
Hacer trampa means 'to cheat' — literally 'to do a trap'. A cheat is un tramposo or una tramposa.

phrases.en: What are we doing this weekend?
phrases.note: Finde is slang for fin de semana, used a lot by young people in Spain.
Aburrida is for a girl — a boy says aburrido. Careful: soy aburrida means 'I'm boring'!
No hay nada = 'there's nothing'. Spanish is happy with double negatives: no + nada.
Spanish has no single word for 'lie-in', so you say 'stay sleeping until late'. Hasta tarde = 'until late'.

phrases.ph: meh PWEH-doh keh-DAHR ehn lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Quedarse = 'to stay'. The me can go before puedo or on the end: ¿puedo quedarme? Both are fine.
Tengo que + verb = 'I have to'. Spanish says ir (go) here, because you're going from where you are.
Algo = 'something'. Divertido = 'fun' — not 'diverted'! Algo + describing word: algo nuevo, algo rico.

phrases.en: I don't want to go for a walk.
phrases.es: No quiero ir a dar un paseo.
phrases.ph: noh KYEH-roh eer ah dahr oon pah-SEH-oh
phrases.note: Dar un paseo = 'go for a walk' — literally 'give a walk'. Pasear means the same thing in one word.
Ya = 'already' — it makes it sound like 'sorry, I'm busy'. Planes is just 'plans'.
Quedar con = 'to meet up with' — very Spanish. Amigas for girl friends; a mixed group is amigos.
Un rollo = 'a drag' in Spain. ¡Qué rollo! = 'how boring!' — you'll hear it constantly.

phrases.en: It's the weekend, leave me alone.
phrases.note: Finde is slang for fin de semana. Dejadme is for talking to more than one person — to one it's déjame. A bit rude!
A domicilio = 'delivered to your home'. Often people just say ¿pedimos algo? — 'shall we order something?'
En casa = 'at home' — no 'the' or 'my' needed. Ir a casa = 'go home'.
Cumpleaños is 'completes years' (cumple + años). People often just say ¡Felicidades! too.

phrases.en: What do you want for your birthday?
phrases.note: Por tu cumpleaños = for your birthday. Friends often shorten it to tu cumple.
Literally 'ask for a wish' — pedir means 'to ask for'. Deseo is a wish.
Soplar means 'to blow' and velas are candles. Vela also means a sail on a boat.
Feliz means happy. The big family meal in Spain is usually on Christmas Eve, called Nochebuena ('good night').
Don't forget the squiggle on año (year) — without it, ano means something very rude! In Spain people eat 12 grapes at midnight.
Spanish says 'make a party' (hacer una fiesta), not 'have' one. Vamos a = 'we're going to'.

phrases.en: Who do you want to invite?
phrases.note: The little a before quién is needed when asking 'who' about a person something is done to. Invitar is easy — it's 'invite'.
Firmar is 'to sign' and tarjeta is a card (a bank card is also tarjeta). Has is 'have you', with a silent h.
Regalo is a present — regalar means 'to give as a gift'. Abre comes from abrir (to open).

phrases.en: I can't believe you're fifteen already!
phrases.es: ¡No me puedo creer que ya tengas quince años!
phrases.ph: noh meh PWEH-doh kreh-EHR keh yah TEHN-gahs KEEN-theh AH-nyohs
phrases.note: Spanish says you 'have' years: tener quince años. In Spain the c in quince is said like 'th'.

phrases.es: Vamos a cantarle el cumpleaños feliz.
phrases.ph: BAH-mohs ah kahn-TAHR-leh ehl koom-pleh-AH-nyohs feh-LEETH
phrases.note: The song is called Cumpleaños feliz — the words are the other way round. The -le on cantarle means 'to him/her'.
¿Qué se dice? = 'what do we say?' — what every Spanish parent asks to get a gracias out of you.

phrases.es: Dale las gracias a la abuela.
phrases.ph: DAH-leh lahs GRAH-thyahs ah lah ah-BWEH-lah
phrases.note: Dar las gracias = 'to say thank you' (literally 'give the thanks'). Dale = 'give her'.
Todavía = 'yet' or 'still'. After no, abre changes to abras — that's how Spanish says 'don't'.

phrases.en: Don't invite too many people, OK?
phrases.ph: noh een-BEE-tehs ah MOO-chah HEHN-teh, BAH-leh
phrases.note: Gente = 'people' but it's singular in Spanish: mucha gente, not muchas. ¿Vale? = 'OK?'.

phrases.es: La fiesta acaba a las once.
phrases.ph: lah FYEHS-tah ah-KAH-bah ah lahs OHN-theh
phrases.note: Acabar = 'to finish'. Times use a las: a las once, a las diez y media.

phrases.en: Who's going to clear all this up?
phrases.ph: kyehn bah ah rreh-koh-HEHR TOH-doh EHS-toh
phrases.note: Recoger = 'to tidy up / clear away'. Todo esto = 'all this' — say it while pointing at the mess.

phrases.en: Go and get changed, the guests are coming.
phrases.es: Ve a cambiarte, que ya vienen los invitados.
phrases.ph: beh ah kahm-BYAHR-teh, keh yah BYEH-nehn lohs een-bee-TAH-dohs
phrases.note: Cambiarse = 'to get changed'. Los invitados = 'the guests' — from invitar, 'to invite'.

phrases.en: Don't eat all the crisps before they get here.
phrases.es: No te comas todas las patatas antes de que lleguen.
phrases.ph: noh teh KOH-mahs TOH-dahs lahs pah-TAH-tahs AHN-tehs deh keh YEH-gehn
phrases.note: In Spain crisps are patatas (or patatas fritas). Comerse todo = 'to eat the whole lot'.
¿Puedo + verb? = 'Can I...?'. A sleepover party is una fiesta de pijamas.
Spanish says 'the presents' (los regalos) where English says 'my presents' — it's obvious whose they are.

phrases.en: I'd like new trainers for my birthday.
phrases.es: Para mi cumpleaños quiero unas zapatillas nuevas.
phrases.ph: PAH-rah mee koom-pleh-AH-nyohs KYEH-roh OO-nahs thah-pah-TEE-yahs NWEH-bahs
phrases.note: Zapatillas is the Spain word for trainers (it can also mean slippers). Swap in whatever you want after quiero.

phrases.en: When are we putting the tree up?
phrases.note: Poner (to put) covers 'put up' here. The full name is el árbol de Navidad (Christmas tree).
Quedan means 'are left'. ¿Cuánto queda? on its own is a handy 'how long is left?'.
In Spain a birthday cake is una tarta. Pastel is used for smaller cakes and pastries.
Gracias por = thanks for. Use it for anything: gracias por la cena, gracias por venir.
Regalar = 'to give as a present'; un regalo is 'a present'. Habéis is for both parents — to one it's has.
Me encanta = 'I love it' for things. Stronger than me gusta. For lots of things: me encantan.

phrases.en: It's not what I asked for.
phrases.es: No es lo que te pedí.
phrases.ph: noh ehs loh keh teh peh-DEE
phrases.note: Pedir = 'to ask for'. Lo que = 'what' in the middle of a sentence. A bit ungrateful — mind who hears it!
Put a before a person's name after invitar: invitar a Lucía, invitar a mis amigas. Swap in any name.

phrases.ph: KWAHN-doh ehs mee FYEHS-tah deh koom-pleh-AH-nyohs
phrases.note: Cumpleaños = 'birthday' — literally 'completes years'. People often shorten it to cumple.
Decorar = 'to decorate' (for a party). For painting a room you'd say pintar instead.
Ilusión = 'excitement' here, not 'illusion'. ¡Qué ilusión! is what Spaniards really say. Careful: excitada sounds rude.
Ganas = 'wanting' or 'eagerness'. Add de + thing: ¡qué ganas de fiesta!
Spanish also says ¡Es mi cumple! — cumple is the everyday short form.
Cantéis is 'don't sing' to more than one person — to one it's no cantes.
Vergüenza = 'embarrassment' — not 'pregnant', that's embarazada! Me dais = 'you (all) give me'.

phrases.ph: PWEH-dehn keh-DAHR-seh ah dohr-MEER mees ah-MEE-gahs
phrases.note: Quedarse a dormir = 'to sleep over'. Una fiesta de pijamas is 'a sleepover party'.

phrases.en: Can you stay upstairs during the party?
phrases.es: ¿Os podéis quedar arriba durante la fiesta?
phrases.ph: ohs poh-DAYS keh-DAHR ah-RREE-bah doo-RAHN-teh lah FYEHS-tah
phrases.note: Arriba = 'upstairs', abajo = 'downstairs'. Os podéis is for both parents.
Cansada is for a girl — ask a boy ¿Estás cansado? Tiredness uses estar because it's a passing state.

phrases.en: What time are you going to bed?
phrases.es: ¿A qué hora te vas a la cama?
phrases.ph: ah keh OH-rah teh bahs ah lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Irse a la cama = 'to go (off) to bed'. The te with vas gives it the sense of heading off — te vas = 'you're off'.

phrases.en: You need to go to bed.
phrases.es: Tienes que irte a la cama.
phrases.ph: TYEH-nehs keh EER-teh ah lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Tienes que + verb = 'you have to...'. A pattern worth knowing: tienes que comer, tienes que estudiar.
Literally 'it's making itself late'. Hacerse = 'to become', so se está haciendo = 'it's becoming'.
In Spain secondary school is el instituto (or el insti for short). Colegio is usually a primary school.

phrases.en: Go and get ready for bed.
phrases.note: Ve a + action = 'go and...'. Prepararte is 'get yourself ready', and para dormir means 'for sleeping'.
Spanish says 'wash your teeth' — lavarte los dientes. Cepillarse los dientes (brush) exists but is less common.
Te has lavado = 'have you washed'. The te shows you're doing it to yourself, so it's los dientes, not tus dientes.
Deja means 'leave' — so 'leave the phone'. Add ya ('now') for more urgency: Deja ya el móvil.
Pon is the short command from poner (to put). A cargar = 'to charge', so 'put the phone to charge'.
Apagar = 'switch off', encender = 'switch on'. In Spain the z in luz is said like the 'th' in 'bath'.

phrases.es: No te quedes despierta hasta muy tarde.
phrases.ph: noh teh KEH-dehs dehs-PYEHR-tah AHS-tah mwee TAHR-deh
phrases.note: Literally 'don't stay awake until very late'. Despierta is for a girl — say despierto to a boy.
Sigues (from seguir, 'to carry on') is the easy way to say 'still': ¿Sigues aquí? = 'Are you still here?'
Just ¿Por qué? in front of the last question. To a boy it's ¿Por qué sigues despierto?
From dormirse ('to fall asleep'). The o in dormir changes to ue here — duerme — so it starts with a 'dwair' sound.
Always plural: 'good nights'. It's also 'good evening' when you arrive somewhere after dark.
Que + a wish = 'may you...'. Reuse it: Que lo pases bien (have a good time), Que te mejores (get well soon).
Mañana means both 'tomorrow' and 'morning'. Hasta mañana = 'until tomorrow', the normal bedtime goodbye.

phrases.en: Did you have a good day?
phrases.note: Bueno drops the -o before a masculine noun: un buen día, not un bueno día. Same with buen chico.
Ponte = 'put on (yourself)' — used for any clothes. Pijama is usually singular in Spain, and the j sounds like a throaty h.
Meterse = 'to get into' somewhere: métete en la ducha (get in the shower), métete en el coche.
El despertador is 'the alarm clock' — from despertar (to wake up). Puesto is the odd 'put/set' form of poner.
Abajo = 'downstairs' (literally 'below'); arriba = 'upstairs'. No need for a separate word for stairs.

phrases.es: Diez minutos y apagas la luz.
phrases.ph: dyehth mee-NOO-tohs ee ah-PAH-gahs lah looth
phrases.note: Spanish often gives orders with plain 'you do' verbs: y apagas la luz = 'and you turn off the light'. Firm but friendly.

phrases.ph: loh TYEH-nehs TOH-doh LEES-toh PAH-rah mah-NYAH-nah
phrases.note: Here listo matches todo (everything), so it stays listo even for a girl. Compare ¿Estás lista? about the person.

phrases.en: Do you want a hot chocolate?
phrases.note: Cola Cao is the chocolate drink brand every Spanish family has — people use the name like 'a hot chocolate'.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, people are sleeping.
phrases.es: Haz menos ruido, que están durmiendo.
phrases.ph: ahth MEH-nohs RRWEE-doh, keh ehs-TAHN door-MYEHN-doh
phrases.note: Literally 'make less noise'. Ruido = 'noise'. Durmiendo is 'sleeping' — the o in dormir changes to u here.
Sueño means both 'dream' and 'sleepiness' — tengo sueño = 'I'm sleepy'. Dulce = 'sweet'.
Te quiero is what family and friends say. Te amo is much more intense and saved for romantic partners.
A boy would say cansado. For 'really tired', try estoy muerta de sueño — 'dead with sleepiness'.
Me voy means 'I'm off' (from irse, to leave). Spanish says a la cama — 'to the bed' — where English just says 'to bed'.
To make a sentence negative, just put no in front of the verb. Your brother would say no estoy cansado.

phrases.en: I'm not going to bed yet.
phrases.es: Todavía no me voy a la cama.
phrases.ph: toh-dah-BEE-ah noh meh boy ah lah KAH-mah
phrases.note: Todavía no means 'not yet' and goes at the start. It's a really useful pair: todavía no lo he hecho = 'I haven't done it yet'.
Tan means 'that/so' before a describing word: no es tan tarde. Tarde means 'late' — and also 'afternoon'.
Word order flips: 'five minutes more'. In Spain the c in cinco is said like the th in 'think'.
Estoy + -ando/-iendo = 'I'm ...ing' right now. Terminando is from terminar (to finish). Add ya: ya estoy terminando.
Ducharme is 'to shower myself' — the -me on the end means 'myself'. Voy a + verb = 'I'm going to...'
Cargador comes from cargar (to charge/load). Mi means 'my' — no accent. With an accent, mí means 'me'.
In Spain el pijama is one thing, so it's mi pijama, not 'pyjamas'. Visto means 'seen' (from ver) — a spelling to learn.

phrases.en: Can you turn the light off?
phrases.note: Apagar means 'to switch off'; the opposite is encender. In Spain the z at the end of luz sounds like th in 'bath'.
Cierra is from cerrar (to close) — the e changes to ie. Said to a parent, add por favor or it sounds like an order.
Deja is from dejar (to leave something). Abierta ends in -a to match la puerta; 'a bit open' is un poco abierta.
Always plural: buenas noches. It also works as 'good evening' when you arrive somewhere after dark.
Hasta means 'until' — 'until tomorrow'. Mañana also means 'morning', so hasta mañana works as 'see you in the morning' too.
Dormir means 'to sleep' — think 'dormitory'. No puedo + verb = 'I can't...', easy to reuse.
Pesadilla ('nightmare') comes from pesado, 'heavy'. The ll sounds like an English y. A normal dream is un sueño.

phrases.en: Can you wake me up at seven?
phrases.note: Despertar means 'to wake someone'. Spanish often uses the simple 'you wake me?' form as a relaxed request. Times use a las: a las siete.
Puesto means 'put' (from poner) — Spanish 'puts' an alarm rather than setting it. Ya adds 'already'.
Literally '(I hope) that you rest'. Que descanses is a warm goodnight wish, common in Spain alongside buenas noches.

phrases.en: Can I read for a bit?
phrases.note: Un rato means 'a while/a bit' — super useful: un rato más = 'a bit longer'. Leer has two e's, each said separately.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.ph: PWEH-deh dohr-MEER MOHN-tee ehn mee ah-bee-tah-THYOHN
phrases.note: Habitación is the usual Spain word for bedroom (the h is silent). Puede = 'can he', so the dog's name can come after the verb.

phrases.en: I'm cold, can I have another blanket?
phrases.ph: TEHN-goh FREE-oh, meh dahs OH-trah MAHN-tah
phrases.note: Otra means 'another' — never say una otra. ¿Me das...? ('Will you give me...?') is the everyday way to ask for something.

phrases.en: What time do I have to get up?
phrases.es: ¿A qué hora me tengo que levantar?
phrases.ph: ah keh OH-rah meh TEHN-goh keh leh-bahn-TAHR
phrases.note: Tengo que + verb = 'I have to...'. Levantarse ('to get up') keeps its me at the front here: me tengo que levantar.
